verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that iḥkām, definitiveness, and tafṣīl, elaboration, concern the Qurʾan’s meanings rather than its wording. Tafṣīl separates what is joined, while iḥkām joins a thing’s parts into an undivided whole. Thus, despite their diverse subjects and purposes, all Qurʾanic verses return to one simple, unified original meaning; every particular purpose is an embodiment of that governing purpose. The Qurʾan may address religious principles, created realities, or legal rulings, and may move from uṣūl to furūʿ and furūʿ al-furūʿ, yet its essential meaning and goal remain unchanged. Its diverse teachings in belief, morals, and deeds are elaborations of, and return to, this single spirit.

That principle is pure tawḥīd. In belief it requires affirming God’s beautiful names and lofty attributes; in ethics, acquiring noble qualities and avoiding vile ones; and in action, doing righteous deeds and avoiding what God forbids. Pure monotheism entails all that the Book teaches at these levels, and none of these levels can be fulfilled without it. The verse therefore shows how the distinct teachings and rulings of the Qurʾan, while retaining their individual character, all derive from one principle and yield rulings proper to each case.

Al-Mizan takes “A Book” to mean “This is a Book,” namely the recited Qurʾan divided into sūrahs and verses. This does not conflict with identifying it with the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), since the recited Qurʾan is identical with what is in the Tablet just as revelation (tanzīl) is identical with interpretation (taʾwīl). “Then” (thumma) indicates progression in the arrangement of discourse, not temporal succession, since the discussion concerns primary and secondary meanings, or generality and particularity.

The commentary rejects several other readings. The claim that definitiveness means immunity from abrogation by a later scripture lacks evidence for that restriction, while abrogation among Qurʾanic verses is undeniable. Reading definitiveness as commands and prohibitions and elaboration as promises and threats is arbitrary; reading them as inimitable eloquence followed by explanation has the same defect. To call the verses firm and free from flaw, then interpret fuṣṣilat as their successive occurrence, is linguistically uncustomary unless fuṣṣilat means division and multiplication, which returns to Al-Mizan’s interpretation. Likewise, taking the verse to mean that the whole Qurʾan was later divided and gradually revealed concerns a different matter, for verses concerning descent better establish that the Qurʾan has a station with God beyond human comprehension before being sent down in a form people can understand. Nor can definitiveness belong to general verses and elaboration to separate clarifying verses, because the verse attributes both qualities to the same verses.

The Qurʾan’s verses therefore possess unity and simplicity in their meanings as well as multiplicity and complexity; this is not the question of taʾwīl and tanzīl. “All-wise” (al-ḥakīm) and “all-aware” (al-khabīr) are divine names of action: the former signifies God’s proficiency in creation, and the latter His knowledge of the particular states of beings and what benefits them. Their use indicates a relation to the definitiveness and elaboration of the verses.

Al-Mizan then treats “Worship no one but Allah. I am indeed a warner from Him to you and a bearer of good news” as an explanation of the Book’s definitive and elaborated content. The revealed discourse has one aspect addressed directly to the Messenger, who receives the command to warn, bring good news, and call people; and another addressed to people through him, consisting of the divine message he recites to them. The quoted words are therefore God’s speech describing what people hear in the Messenger’s call, not words of the Messenger being reported and not a shift in address. “Worship no one but Allah” is neither an implied command by the Messenger nor a negation meaning that people do not worship others. Its connection with the following command to seek forgiveness and repent shows that it is a prohibition: worship of every alleged partner is forbidden, and worship is restricted to God alone.

verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains that, after people accept God as their Lord by renouncing the worship of others, they are commanded to seek His forgiveness and turn to Him through righteous deeds. This is the path to nearness to God: abandoning other gods, seeking forgiveness and purification, and returning to Him in action. The preceding prohibition of worshipping anyone but God marks the fundamental stage of monotheism, while seeking forgiveness and repentance belong to the subsidiary stage of righteous works. Warnings and glad tidings depend upon tawḥīd, but the promised fruits follow only when this root is complete and produces its branches.

More specifically, the commentary holds that “turn to Him penitently” apparently means faith (īmān): people should abandon idol worship, seek forgiveness for their sins, and then believe in their Lord. This accounts for joining istighfār to tawba with thumma. It rejects as strained the view that one seeks forgiveness as an end and achieves it through repentance, as well as the readings that distinguish past sins from future sins or reduce thumma to “and” on the ground that repentance and forgiveness are identical.

“A good provision for a specified term” means a good worldly life until the fixed end of one’s life. Worldly provision is good only when it leads toward the happiness prepared for human beings, including security, comfort, dignity, and nobility; it is the opposite of the wretched life of one who disregards God’s remembrance. Wealth and worldly standing without faith and God’s patronage (wilāya) are not truly good, since they leave one in an animalistic life of greed, gluttony, predation, rivalry, and ignorance. A free soul rejects such a life even if this entails poverty or humiliation. For an individual, the good life is moderation in material enjoyment guided by useful knowledge and good deeds. For a righteous community, it is shared enjoyment of God’s earthly blessings through compassion, cooperation, and solidarity, with each person finding personal benefit in the community’s welfare rather than worshipping himself or enslaving others.

Regarding “grant His grace (faḍla-hu) to every meritorious person (kulla dhī faḍl),” faḍl means excess or increase. Although some suggest that the pronoun in “His grace” may refer to the meritorious person, the meaning is that God grants an increased recompense to each person who excels in moral virtue, righteous works, or special qualities, without depriving anyone of his merit or giving it to another. Al-Mizan contrasts this with societies divided between a dominant, arrogant class and an oppressed class, a disparity it holds can be rectified only by the religion of monotheism. By reserving divinity and sovereignty for God, it places strong and weak, great and small, black and white, and male and female on equal footing, while preserving the distinctions due to actual merit.

The first promise thus concerns a general provision shared by society—its good public life—whereas the second recognizes advantages earned through individual virtue. The former concerns worldly enjoyment; the latter concerns recompense in the hereafter, or the assignment in this world and the next of what each person’s excellence deserves. Equality does not mean treating the superior and inferior alike, cancelling individual distinctions, or equating the diligent worker with the lazy or the serious worker with one occupied in trivialities.

Al-Mizan reads wa in tawallaw as direct address: although tawallaw could be read as a third-person perfect verb, ʿalaykum and the surrounding discourse establish the sense of tatawallaw, “if you turn away.” It rejects a commentator’s claim that the promise of good provision proves that the Muslim community will be spared annihilating punishment. No evidence establishes this, and widespread outward profession of Islam does not mean that all humanity believed or that professed faith was free of hypocrisy. If the faith of only part of a people were enough to avert annihilation, the same would have protected the peoples called by Noah, Hūd, and others, who preached the same call and promise; yet punishment came upon them, while God justly saved the believers. The cited commentator’s appeal to Sūrah Yūnus is likewise unsupported. Al-Mizan maintains that God judges between this community and its Prophet, punishes the deniers, and saves the believers, in accordance with His unchanging practice among His servants.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that the verse grounds the preceding warning in the Resurrection. If people turn from exclusive worship of God and reject His partners, they face the punishment of the terrible day, which is the Day of Resurrection: they will return to God after death, and His power over all things includes reviving them. The closing phrase removes doubt about resurrection after death. Al-Qummī narrates in his Tafsīr that the punishment of the terrible day refers to the Smoke and the Cry.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan explains yathnūn as folding or bending back. The idolaters fold their chests and lower their heads to hide from the Qurʾan when it is recited, in reality avoiding the Prophet so that they need not answer his arguments. Covering their heads with their garments accompanies this attempt, but God knows alike what they conceal and disclose; hiding therefore neither protects them from the Qurʾan nor escapes His knowledge of their private and public lives.

The commentary considers it a meritorious alternative that the garments refer to their covering themselves at night in bed: even in that most concealed state, God knows them. It rejects as remote from the context interpretations which make the object of their hiding God or the Prophet, or make the folding of breasts a folding of hearts in disbelief or enmity.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan holds that dābba here includes everything that moves, because the verse displays the comprehensiveness of God’s knowledge. Every earthly creature depends upon God’s sustenance and could not exist without it. His knowing its mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ explains this provision: He knows every creature’s condition and the place where it settles, whether fixed, and the place in which it temporarily lodges before departing or returning. Provision reaches its recipient only through the Provider’s knowledge of its permanent or transitory condition and residence.

Thus, mustaqarr is the place in which a creature remains during its earthly life, and mustawdaʿ the place where it dwells and then leaves. Interpretations that make them respectively life and death, loins and wombs, or actual and merely potential existence are far from the context, unless the clause is treated as independent rather than explanatory.

The commentary further maintains that rizq belongs solely to God. It is not problematic to say that provision is due from Him, since He Himself has undertaken this obligation. Since a creature’s existence proceeds from His bounty, what sustains that existence must also be from Him; and as no one shares in creating the creature, no one shares in providing its sustenance. For the meaning of kitāb mubīn, the commentary refers to its earlier discussions.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan takes the heavens and earth created in six days to be the visible material layers above and surrounding the earth, with “above” and “below” always relative. The nearest heaven is adorned with stars and planets, while the Qurʾan describes the seven heavens above it only as layered one over another. The earth’s spherical form is also indicated by the night’s covering being drawn over the day.

The “days” are measurable periods, not necessarily terrestrial days. The heavens, initially smoke, were separated and arranged into seven heavens in two periods; the earth was formed in two, and its means of sustenance were ordained in four, referring to the four seasons. The heavens and earth in their present form thus came not from absolute nothingness but from an undifferentiated composite mass, whose parts were gathered, divided, and separated. The remaining two of the six periods concern the rest of creation. Since all living things are made from water, water is the substance of life.

“His Throne was upon the waters” is an adverbial statement about that creation. The Throne is a metaphor for God’s all-encompassing sovereignty and management, and its being established upon the water signifies His sovereignty over the substance of life. The interpretation of ʿarsh as a physical structure does not suit this context.

The purposive clause, “that He may test you,” means that creation distinguishes the good in conduct from the bad. Trial leads to this distinction, which in turn bears the consequences of reward and punishment and the fulfilment of God’s true promise. Creation may accordingly be described through several connected purposes, including trial, discrimination between good and evil, requital, fulfilment of the promise, and the worship for which jinn and humankind were created. These purposes do not conflict, since the interconnected order of the world makes each created kind an outcome and purpose of the others.

Human beings are the most perfected material creatures; when perfected in knowledge and good deeds, they attain the highest rank. As the perfect is the end intended through the imperfect, the absolutely best person in deeds is the true purpose behind the heavens and earth. Al-Mizan says this explains the ḥadīth qudsī in which God tells the Prophet, “Were it not for you, I would not have created the firmament” (law lā-ka lammā khalaqtu al-aflāk): he is the best of creation.

Majmaʿ al-Bayān reports al-Jubāʾī’s view that a morally accountable being must already have existed when the Throne was upon the waters, since that creation otherwise yielded no benefit; it also reports ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā’s reply, preferred by Sayyid al-Murtaḍā, that informing later accountable people of it can itself benefit them. Al-Mizan rejects the underlying Muʿtazilī premise that God’s acts are governed by a purpose external to Him or by the production of benefit. Goodness and benefit motivate created agents because they are concepts derived from the created cosmic order; they cannot precede that order or govern its Creator. God alone decides and creates all things.

Yet the Qurʾanic purposes of creation indicate benefits that follow from divine acts. God perfects what He creates, and no evil or ugliness originates from Him. This does not mean that good is merely whatever proceeds from or is commanded by God, even where reason judges it repugnant, nor that evil is simply whatever He has not commanded.

Finally, the test points to resurrection. The faithless dismiss not only the Qurʾan’s eloquence as magic but also its truthful teaching of resurrection after death, displaying their obstinate rejection of truth. Although siḥr might be taken figuratively as deceptive presentation of falsehood as truth, this does not accord with the apparent sense in the comparable Qurʾanic context.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan explains the emphatic verse as an oath that, if God mercifully delays the punishment deserved by the disbelievers, they mockingly ask what prevents its descent. Their question shows that they had heard the threat of an inescapable punishment but derided its delay. God answers that when it overtakes them, no one will turn it away and the very punishment they mocked will encompass them.

The phrase ilā umma maʿdūda most plainly means “until a specified time.” It may also mean for the sake of a specified community: God will support the religion through righteous people whose faith cannot be impaired, enabling believers to practise the religion He approves. The commentary accepts this alternative. It rejects readings in which umma is a later people whom God punishes, or whose disobedience brings the Day of Judgement, because the verse plainly makes the mockers themselves the people punished.

Their mockery amounts to saying that, since they will not abandon disbelief, a genuine punishment should come immediately; its delay supposedly proves the threat false. The answer is that it will surely come and cannot be repelled. The threatened punishment apparently includes a worldly punishment that descends upon and engulfs them, in addition to punishment in the Hereafter. Thus, as they call resurrection “plain magic,” they also ridicule the delayed threat by asking, “What holds it back?”
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains that “tasting” portrays the fleeting character of granted pleasures, while withdrawal means removing what was in one’s possession, and yaʾūs is the certainty that a desired thing will not occur. God calls blessings “mercy” because they fulfil human needs without being deserved or owed.

When God grants a person a blessing and then takes it away, that person becomes hopeless of its restoration and ungrateful, treating the blessing as an inherent right rather than God’s gift. The use of “man” makes this despair over what is lost and ingratitude toward the Giver a tendency of the human species.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan explains naʿmāʾ as a favour visibly manifest in its recipient, darrāʾ as a visible harm, and sayyiʾāt here as distressing calamities. When prosperity follows adversity, man declares that his troubles have gone, imagining they cannot return. He then becomes an exultant braggart: he would not rejoice so recklessly if he knew that blessings are transient, not under his control, and that former hardships may return. His boastfulness likewise shows that he regards the blessings as honours securely possessed by himself rather than gifts that can be taken away.

These reactions, together with despair and ingratitude when blessings are withdrawn, arise from human short-sightedness. A person forgets that God gave what was removed and can restore it, so adversity does not lead him to steadfast hope and supplication. When prosperity returns, he takes it as his due, fails to thank God, and boasts over others.

The exception is those who are patient and do righteous deeds. Patience prevents hardship from producing despair and ingratitude; righteous action means thanking God when adversity is removed and using His blessings in ways pleasing to Him and beneficial to His creatures, rather than in self-sufficient exultation and boasting. God promises such people forgiveness, which removes the traces of this blameworthy tendency and replaces them with praiseworthy qualities, and a great reward.

The promise also shows that patience joined to righteous deeds is inseparable from faith, since forgiveness is not granted to idolaters. The same promise is made to believers and to those who fear their Lord in secret. In the present sequence, these verses expose the disbelievers’ natural assumption that their blessings will not end in punishment and that their miseries will not be transformed into the good life God has promised.

verses.12:
Al-Mizan reads this verse hypothetically. Given the manifest truth, proofs, and arguments brought by the Prophet, the idolaters’ denial is so improbable that possible explanations are raised only to refute them: perhaps he omitted part of the revelation for fear of their demands, or perhaps they allege that he fabricated it. The next verse’s challenge to produce ten fabricated chapters completes the second branch. These possibilities neither charge the Prophet with failing to convey the message nor console him for grief; they prepare the decisive clarification that he is only a warner and God governs the matter.

The verse thus supposes that he may have withheld some revealed passages because he feared that they would demand a treasure or an angel. Such an omission would leave the truth incompletely disclosed, since parts of the Qurʾan clarify and reinforce one another: argumentative verses clarify claims, promises and threats encourage acceptance, and stories and parables move hearts. Al-Mizan takes the pronoun in “be upset by it” (ḍāʾiq bihi ṣadruka an yaqūlū) to refer to the part revealed, not to their demand itself: perhaps he would leave it aside for fear that they would say, “Why has not a treasure been sent down to him, or not an angel accompany him?” The alternative interpretation that the verse forbids and consoles the Prophet over their rejection does not fit the context.

“You are only a warner” answers their arbitrary demands for extraordinary signs. The Prophet, as a human messenger, has been charged with delivering a warning and cannot produce the requested signs unless God wills and authorizes them. “Allah is a trustee over all things” completes the answer: God alone originates and manages every affair, whether it follows the ordinary course or breaks it. A wakīl is entrusted with and manages an affair; therefore, the idolaters ask the Prophet for what belongs to God alone.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan says that “or” may continue the preceding hypothetical question: did the Prophet omit revelation for fear of their demands, or do they say that he fabricated it? Some commentators instead take it as detached, meaning simply, “Rather, they say that he invented it.”

The command to bring ten fabricated chapters like it answers their accusation directly. If the Qurʾan were something the Prophet had produced and falsely attributed to God, others could produce its like; they are therefore told to seek the help of every being besides God. “Like it” refers to the Qurʾan, or to a chapter as part of it. The challenge is not restricted to arrangement or Arabic eloquence, for it includes all whom they can invoke, including those without Arabic fluency. It concerns the Qurʾan’s truthful teachings, arguments, proofs, admonitions, morals, knowledge of the unseen, as well as its eloquence.

Its miraculousness consequently cannot lie in eloquence, clarity, or composition alone. If it did, the inclusion of non-Arabs and the general summons to all possible helpers would be pointless; the argument that a text from other than God would contain much discrepancy would not address the mostly intellectual contradictions that do not impair eloquence; and the apparent sequence of challenges to one chapter and then ten would be unsuitable. One proposed solution is that the order of revelation of these challenge-verses differed from their placement in the sūrahs; Al-Mizan finds this possible only if the claimed order of revelation is accepted. It concludes that the Qurʾan is miraculous in all its distinctive attributes: eloquence, clear expression, true teachings, ethics, laws, narratives, parables, knowledge of the unseen, power over hearts, and beauty.

Majmaʿ al-Bayān, reporting al-Ṭabrisī, explains the varying challenges—one chapter, ten chapters, or a discourse—as variations in the quantity of speech through which its miraculous arrangement is challenged. Al-Mizan accepts that more or less may in principle be demanded, but finds this inadequate to explain a demand for ten after one if eloquence alone is in question. Other scholars say that several long chapters are needed to reproduce together the Qurʾan’s knowledge, rulings, stories, eloquence, and freedom from discrepancy; on the basis of traditions, they identify nine such earlier chapters which, with Sūrah Hūd, make ten. Al-Mizan objects that traditions establishing the order of revelation are solitary reports, often unreliable, and should not bear exegetical argument. The accusation concerns every Qurʾanic chapter, long and short, so the challenge cannot be arbitrarily confined to ten long chapters or the particular chapters listed. Nor does it plausibly refer specifically to Sūrah Hūd.

The relevant “meaning” is not the rhetoricians’ mental arrangement of ideas, since eloquent lies, jest, obscenity, satire, and fabrication also possess such meaning. Rather, it is the Qurʾan’s true divine purpose: guidance free from falsehood, a decisive criterion and clarification, healing and mercy for believers, and judgment in human disagreement. A ḥadīth must convey a significant purpose, and a sūrah is a collection of verses united by a distinctive divine purpose; the challenge is not met by matching disconnected individual verses with isolated Arabic phrases.

The forms of challenge correspond to different manifestations of this quality. The whole Qurʾan contains what humanity needs until the Day of Resurrection, including fundamental knowledge, noble ethics, and subsidiary laws. A single sūrah comprehensively expounds one divine purpose in guidance. A multiplicity of sūrahs displays a variety of purposes and modes of exposition. “Ten” apparently signifies abundance rather than the literal number, so the demand is for a recognized multitude of equivalent chapters. “Let them bring a discourse like it” (52:34) embraces all these forms, since a discourse may be the whole Qurʾan, one sūrah, or many.

An opponent might claim that inability to produce even one sūrah proves only the Prophet’s unmatched human genius. Al-Mizan replies that, although a human may excel beyond others in a natural quality, others can follow, practise, and imitate some of what he does. If the Qurʾan were his speech, others could at least imitate a chapter, even if not the whole. A single Qurʾanic chapter’s profound eloquence, truthful meaning, noble attributes, and freedom from falsehood cannot arise by coincidence; a succession of such chapters, each disclosing a purpose and a secret, makes coincidence still more impossible.

The qualifier “fabricated,” unique to this challenge, possibly reflects its link with the conclusion that the Qurʾan was sent down with Allah’s knowledge. The challenge is to fabricate chapters containing divine knowledge inaccessible to anyone but God, which fabrication itself cannot accomplish. Finally, the demand is for something “like” the Qurʾan rather than better than it because an equivalent would suffice to disprove a miraculous sign. Human speech, even the speech of an unrivalled person, should be imitable to some degree; the inability to produce its like therefore removes the claim that the Qurʾan is merely the Prophet’s speech.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan holds that this continues the Prophet’s commanded speech to the idolaters. “They” are the idols and all the other helpers whom the idolaters were told to invoke. If their deities, eloquent speakers, People of the Book, soothsayers, learned people, and all others from whom help might be sought cannot respond, the idolaters must know that the Qurʾan was revealed with God’s knowledge, not produced from the Prophet’s knowledge or taught to him by another. They must also know that monotheism is true: had another deity existed, it would have helped them oppose the book that was to defeat and erase those deities.

Their helpers’ failure establishes the idolaters’ own inability to meet the challenge even with every resource they suppose available. “Sent down with Allah’s knowledge” means the unique knowledge of the Unseen (al-ghayb), inaccessible to anyone except by God’s permission. It means that the Qurʾan contains knowledge known only to God, who revealed it to make its guidance and true knowledge understood. Interpretations that reduce the phrase to God’s awareness that He revealed it, to His awareness of its inimitability, or to His knowledge of its composition are weak.

Two conclusions follow from the non-response of their invoked patrons. First, a being that does not answer those who call upon it in a matter so vital to its own supposed divinity is not truly a god; the true Deity answers the distressed caller. Second, once the Qurʾan is established as God’s truthful revelation and it declares that there is no god but Him, that declaration must be affirmed. “Will you, then, submit?” is therefore a command to submit to these conclusions, phrased as a question.

The commentary rejects readings that address the Prophet through an honorific second-person plural, since classical Arabic reserves such a plural of status for the speaker’s first person, not “you” or “they.” Moreover, the Prophet inherently knows divine revelation as God’s speech and needs no evidence from opponents’ failure to establish it; nor would it make sense to invite him to acknowledge God’s oneness or submit. It likewise rejects readings addressed to believers, even if amended to mean that they should strengthen their certainty. Such readings arbitrarily restrict the verse and rest on an incomplete argument.

The idolaters’ own silence does not prove the Qurʾan divine, for they may have known it was true while resisting it, despaired of their partners’ help, or spoken frivolously rather than seriously attempting the challenge. Only the failure of helpers after being invoked could establish the point, and the verse does not state that the idolaters themselves made such an invocation. Thus, a reading based on their non-response would require unsupported additions and would ask believers to ground certainty on a non-occurring event, which is unworthy of divine speech.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains tawfiya as giving in full what is due and bakhsh as paying less than the full due. The verses threaten those who reject the truth and choose worldly life and its adornment over the Hereafter. Every action yields the end for which it is intended, provided the other contributing factors obtain. Thus, actions aimed at wealth, beauty, comfort, or other worldly ends may yield their worldly effects, but cannot yield the ends of the Hereafter when those ends were never intended. Even deeds outwardly suited to the Hereafter—righteousness, good conduct, and good character—do not bring its reward or higher rank unless performed to please God and seek His reward.

Their full recompense in this world means the actualization of their actions’ effects according to the causal order governing both material and spiritual realities, not simply the granting of whatever outcome they imagined or desired. They may receive only some of what they seek, since results depend on all their causes and God gives, withholds, advances, and delays according to the order He has established.

In the Hereafter they encounter the reality of such worldly deeds: Fire, which consumes their deeds and worldly attainments as fire consumes fuel. Hence what they accomplished fails and their works come to naught; there is nothing for them but the Fire because every other effect has been invalidated. This is the reality conveyed elsewhere by the designation House of Ruin (Dār al-Bawār).
verses.16:

verses.17:
Al-Mizan reads the opening question as an incomplete rhetorical negation: one who possesses the qualities named is not like heedless people, and the Prophet, to whom the final singular command is directed, therefore must not doubt the Qurʾan. The construction is general in wording and applies to the Prophet in this setting; it neither exclusively identifies “he who” with him nor restricts “it is they who have faith in it” to the Companions.

Bayyina, literally something clear and apparent, may also denote what makes another thing clear, such as a proof, sign, or testimony. Here its context most strongly indicates divine insight, not the Qurʾanic revelation itself or rational argumentation (ḥujjat al-ʿaql). The Prophet stands upon an insight granted by his Lord concerning the truth of the Qurʾan; this does not deny that the Qurʾan can elsewhere itself be called a clear divine sign, since each usage has its context.

The witness (shāhid) is one who testifies to the Qurʾan’s truth, rather than merely observes in order to testify later. He possesses his own certain divine insight, believes on that basis, and confirms both the truth of the revelation and the uprightness of the one standing upon the proof. Such corroborating testimony dispels misgivings and strengthens certainty. Yatlū-hu therefore means “follows,” not “recites”; its pronoun may refer either to the person standing on the proof or to the proof itself, since to follow either is ultimately to follow that same proof. “Of his own” refers to that person, not to his Lord or to the proof. Reports in both Shīʿī and Sunnī ḥadīth collections identifying ʿAlī as the witness are thus understood as applying this general principle to him, not as making him the verse’s exclusive referent. The commentary rejects readings that make the witness the Qurʾan, Gabriel or another aiding angel, the Prophet, or his tongue, as well as readings that treat yatlū-hu as recitation.

The Book of Moses, described as a guide and mercy because it contains authentic teaching and divine ordinances, preceded either the one endowed with insight or his manifest proof. This confirms that the Qurʾan and its bearer are not unprecedented: they follow the established path of prophethood, whose earlier scripture guided people and conveyed mercy. “A guide and mercy” qualifies the Book of Moses, not the witness. The Torah’s precedent, together with the witness’s testimony and the manifest proof, supports the Qurʾan as a continuation and confirmation of a known divine path.

“It is they who have faith in it” refers to those who stand on a manifest proof, and “it” is the Qurʾan, which is itself a proof from God or is supported by one. The same applies to the pronoun in the warning that whoever among the factions denies it will meet the Fire. The verse consequently tells the Prophet that, since he stands on such proof, is supported by a witnessing follower, and is preceded by the Book of Moses, he should not be disturbed by the majority’s rejection. Marya is a kind of doubt, and the emphatic statement that the Qurʾan is “the truth” from his Lord gives the reason for forbidding it: these converging grounds leave no basis for doubt, though most people do not believe.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan holds that the verses may continue the reassurance of the Prophet: since he stands on a clear proof from his Lord, he is no fabricator against God, whereas none is a greater wrongdoer than one who fabricates a lie against Him. To fabricate against God (al-iftirāʾ al-kadhb ʿalā Allāh) is to ascribe to Him what is not His or to make claims about Him falsely and without knowledge. Because the gravity of wrongdoing corresponds to the one wronged, fabrication against God is the greatest wrongdoing.

The accusation that the Prophet invented the Qurʾan is turned back upon the idolaters. By associating partners with the one God, barring people from His path, treating His path as crooked, and choosing another way of life, they imply that His true path is not His and alter the way conveyed through fiṭra and prophethood. By denying the Hereafter while affirming the Origin, they imply that creation has no purpose. Their false religion, false beliefs concerning the Origin and Resurrection, and worldly social path apart from God’s religion of truth are therefore fabrications against Him.

Their being “presented” (ʿaraḍ) before their Lord means that the angels entrusted with them bring them forth for final judgment after the veil has been removed and the truth and divine signs have become manifest; no barrier remains between them and their Lord. The witnesses, whose testimony is given where only truth can be spoken and facts cannot be evaded, declare that these are the people who lied against their Lord. The pronouncement, “Look! The curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers,” is also part of the witnesses’ speech.

This curse on the Day of Judgement is not merely like curse in the world, for this world is the abode of action and that Day the abode of recompense. It is the realization of what they earned: perpetual exclusion from the special mercy reserved for the truly faithful, together with eternal punishment and estrangement from God.

The wrongdoers are those who obstruct God’s way, try to distort it, and deny the Hereafter. Seeking only worldly provision, they disregard the true faith and the religion of human nature. Whether they profess a Creator while following a distorted tradition that departs from Islam, or deny Him altogether, they are wrongdoers and fabricators against God. Al-Mizan concludes that dīn, in Qurʾanic usage, denotes the social norms prevailing in a community; these may conform to the correct natural religion, Islam, or be a distorted departure from God’s way.
