verses.20:
Al-Mizan explains that those who fabricate against God cannot thwart Him on earth. Their deviation from divine servanthood, obstruction and distortion of His way, and lies about Him did not arise because their power or will surpassed God’s, or because they escaped His patronage for another guardian. Their idols and other supposed protectors neither managed their affairs nor compelled their wrongdoing; God alone was their guardian and manager. He recompenses their evil intentions and deeds by drawing them, without their awareness, toward everlasting punishment and by leading astray those who first chose to swerve.

Their punishment is doubled either because they rebelled and persisted in rebellion or because, besides disobeying themselves, they led others into disobedience. They bear the consequences both of what they did and of their effects upon those whom they misled.

Their inability to listen and see means that they could not receive the warnings and glad tidings, heed admonitions concerning the Resurrection, or comprehend God’s signs so as to believe. Though the Qurʾan also attributes this deprivation of hearing, sight, and understanding to God, the disbelievers’ own admission that they failed to listen or reason shows that they brought this deprivation upon themselves through sin and transgression.

The commentary rejects alternatives that construe the phrase as meaning that they could hear and see but refused to use those faculties, refer it to their idols, remove its negation so that it means “so long as they could” hear and see, or take it merely as a metaphor for aversion to the benefits of hearing and sight. Although it calls the last the most proper of these alternatives, it judges all of them unsound and maintains the preceding interpretation.
verses.21: Al-Mizan explains that a human being truly owns only the soul granted by God. Whoever exchanges it for disbelief and sin, thereby ruining and wasting it, has suffered the loss of his soul; this loss is a metaphor for its ruin. What they fabricated were baseless lies born of delusions, claims beautified by base desire, and worldly ambition. When the veil of worldly life is removed, those illusions vanish and their fabrications collapse. They then recognize God as the Manifest Truth and see from Him what they had never expected.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan explains lā jarama as an emphatic expression which came through usage to mean “indeed,” “truly,” or “without fail,” so that the verse decisively declares them the greatest losers in the Hereafter.

They are the greatest losers because denial and obstinacy have ruined their souls and squandered their potential, leaving them no hope of salvation from Hellfire. So long as they persist, they likewise have no prospect of attaining faith’s success and happiness in this world: their hearing, sight, and hearts are sealed because they have made desire their god and have been led astray knowingly.

One might also understand their loss as extending to worldly life, since rejection of God’s path deprives them of the happiness to which true religion leads. Yet their loss in the Hereafter is greater because it is eternal, whereas worldly life is fleeting, and because the consequences of deeds are intensified there. The commentary therefore concludes that the verse most properly confines the designation “greatest losers” to the Hereafter, without affirming it here for this life.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan explains that those promised everlasting Paradise are believers who do righteous deeds and are humble before their Lord (akhbatū ilā Rabbi-him). Al-Rāghib reports that khabat literally denotes firm ground and akhbata originally means seeking or settling upon it; it later came figuratively to signify humility, mildness, meekness, and fearfulness before God.

Here humility before God signifies contentment with Him: faith becomes firm, unwavering, and free of doubt, as firm ground protects what is planted in it. Akhbatū ilā Rabbi-him cannot be read as akhbatū li-Rabbi-him, “humble for the sake of their Lord,” because the meaning of contentment requires ilā rather than li-.

The added qualification of humility identifies a particular group among believers, not believers generally: those content with God and possessing insight from Him. The verses distinguish this group from the spiritually blind. Al-Mizan consequently rejects the view that the seven verses from “Is he who stands on a manifest proof from his Lord” through “Will you not then take admonition?” merely contrast Qurʾan-deniers with Qurʾan-believers.
verses.24: Al-Mizan explains that a mathal is a representation that makes an abstract meaning intelligible through a tangible or relatable example. The two previously described groups are thus compared respectively to one who is blind and deaf and one who sees and hears; they plainly cannot be equal.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains that the common recitation, innī, begins Noah’s speech, while the variant annī carries the implied sense of bi-annī. In either case, Noah’s declaration that he is a manifest warner summarizes his entire mission: all that he conveys from his Lord is clear warning. It also identifies his role more fully: he is God’s messenger, sent only as an intermediary to warn his people of divine punishment.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan takes Noah’s command, “Worship none but Allah,” as an exposition of his being a manifest warner: his mission was to forbid worship of all besides God by warning people of punishment. It rejects readings that make the command merely an apposition to, or object of, his warning, since the context better supports this account of his mission.

“The punishment of a painful day” apparently means the punishment of extermination, though it may include divine punishment generally, rather than specifically the Hereafter. Noah’s people later demand that he bring the threatened punishment, and Noah replies that Allah will bring it if He wishes (11:32–33). The pain is attributed to the day because the setting is described in place of what occurs within it. Nor is this punishment inevitable in the sense that would make Noah’s fear meaningless: fear concerns what may occur.

Noah called them from fear of idols to fear of the true Lord. God, not their false deities, created them, governs their lives, created the heavens and earth, made the sun and moon shine, sends rain, brings forth vegetation, creates gardens, and divides rivers. Since He alone is their Lord, He alone should be worshipped and His punishment alone feared.

Although this is a demonstrative argument grounded in certainty, they received it through conjecture. They imagined God after the model of a human master whose interests must be protected by obedience, offerings, sacrifices, and worship lest his wrath be incurred. In reality, punishment for rejecting God’s worship and arrogantly resisting His Lordship follows the certain order of existence. The weak submit to the strong; much more must all submit to God, the One, the Overpowering, to whom all affairs return.

God has interconnected the parts of the universe in a causal order. When something departs from the course required by the rest of the causes, it disrupts that order; the general causes then act to restore it. If the deviant part corrects itself, it remains; otherwise it is overwhelmed by calamities. Human beings likewise have a course proper to their creation. Following it brings happiness and harmony with the universe, whose heavens and earth yield blessings. This is Islam, the religion appointed for humankind and preached by Noah and all subsequent prophets. Departing from it opposes the cosmic order and brings suffering. If one returns and submits to God’s will, blessings may return after adversity; otherwise destruction and annihilation await, while God is self-sufficient from the worlds.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that the opening fa marks the faithless elite’s hasty rejection of Noah’s message, without reflection on what would benefit them. Rather than answer his argument for monotheism, they deny his prophethood and refuse the obedience it entails. Their response contains two connected claims: they see no evidence requiring them to follow him, and they think the evidence instead shows that he lies.

Their first claim is developed through three repeated appeals to what they “see,” revealing a premise that accepts only what is sensed and rejects the metaphysical. First, they call Noah merely a human like themselves. This is not, as some commentators held, chiefly an assertion of equality in family or social rank; if that were intended, they could simply have said that he was like them, and the statement would duplicate their later denial of his merit. By stressing his humanity, they deny that a human being can be a prophet and infer that they need not follow him.

Second, they say that only the simpleminded riffraff, arādhilunā, follow him. The expression denotes those deemed low, base, and despicable. bādī al-raʾy may qualify these followers as apparently low at first sight, or may mean that they followed Noah on a first, unreflective impression; the latter requires an implicit additional verb. In effect, the elite claim that accepting Noah would associate them with the weak, poor, slaves, and needy, depriving them of dignity and social power. They assume that a true and beneficial call would be embraced by society’s powerful and distinguished, not by its lowly members.

Third, they deny that Noah and his followers possess any faḍl, “merit,” over them. Because the indefinite term occurs under negation, Al-Mizan understands it generally: they deny him both material advantages and unseen superiority, such as knowledge of the Unseen or supernatural support, rather than limiting it to wealth. Their plural address includes his followers, as they seek to draw them back to the elite’s own path. They demand a benefit—worldly wealth, hidden knowledge, or extraordinary power—that would make obedience worthwhile. Noah’s later words, “I do not say to you that I possess the treasuries of Allah, neither do I know the Unseen. I do not claim to be an angel …” (11:31), support this broader understanding.

Their final statement, “Rather we consider you to be liars,” concludes these arguments. Since they perceive neither proof nor worldly prestige in Noah, while he calls them to obey, they suspect that he seeks wealth, property, or leadership through a false claim. Their accusation remains a suspicion rather than a certainty, like the claim that a messenger “seeks to gain an advantage over you …” (23:24).
verses.28:
Al-Mizan presents this verse and the following four as Noah’s ordered answer to the objections of his people. Their argument rested on sensory perception and denial of the metaphysical: they first claimed to find no reason to obey him, then treated what they observed as evidence that they should not obey him. Noah affirms his prophethood, rejects their charge of falsehood, and repeatedly calls them “my people” in an effort to draw them near. The replies answer their objections in a connected threefold sequence: the manifest proof, his refusal to seek material reward or dismiss believers, and his denial of the forms of superiority they expected.

This first reply answers their claim that he was merely a human like themselves, not their accusation that he was lying, their contempt for his followers, or their denial of his merit. Since they denied any human connection with the Unseen, Noah reminds them that prophethood is confirmed by a supernatural sign. Thus the “manifest proof” (bayyina) is a miraculous sign from God establishing the truth of his claim, not merely the prophet’s intuitive knowledge of his own prophethood.

God’s “mercy” apparently means the scripture and knowledge given to Noah, for the Qurʾan calls scripture, knowledge, and divine signs mercy. The phrase “though it should be invisible to you” refers apparently to this mercy: their ignorance and aversion to truth have concealed from them the knowledge and guidance that Noah has made known to them. A variant reading means that God’s mercy has been hidden from them.

“Shall we force it upon you” means compelling them to accept this mercy, believe in God and His signs, and acquire the enlightenment and insight that divine knowledge requires. Noah therefore says in effect that, despite his human nature, he has the miraculous proof and the revealed knowledge needed for his message, but they reject it through stubbornness and arrogance. Having received the proof, they demand something further that would compel belief; yet religion admits no compulsion. The verse thus establishes the rejection of coercion in religion as an ordinance of Noah’s earliest divine law, one that has not been abrogated.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains that Noah first answers the accusation that his call is a lie intended to seize people’s wealth: because he asks no material reward, they have no basis for imputing greed to him.

He then answers their contempt for his followers. Rather than call them “riffraff,” he calls them “those who have faith,” dignifying them through their relation to God. He will not drive them away, because they will encounter their Lord: they will return to God, be judged for their deeds, and receive their recompense from Him. Their judgment belongs to God, not to Noah or to the elite who expect the poor, needy, and weak to be excluded from goodness, dignity, and blessing.

Al-Mizan rejects interpretations that make their encounter with God mean only that God will avenge their expulsion or reward them, since these do not fit the apparent meaning; the first would also make the following verse about God’s help against Noah redundant. Noah’s description of the elite as an ignorant people refers to their ignorance of the Hereafter and of the fact that judgment and recompense belong exclusively to God, not to ignorance merely as foolish conduct or as failure to recognize virtue above wealth and status.
verses.30: Al-Mizan explains that naṣr, “help,” means protection or rescue. Noah asks who could protect him from God’s punishment if he expelled the believers whom his people deride as riffraff. Driving them away would be a grave wrong: God aids the wronged against their oppressors and avenges injustice. Reason itself shows that God does not treat oppressor and oppressed alike, nor leave oppression unrecompensed.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains that Noah answers his people’s denial that he possesses any merit by rejecting the false kind of superiority they expect of a prophet. They assume that a messenger must independently control the treasuries of divine mercy, enrich the poor, heal the sick, revive the dead, govern heaven and earth, know the Unseen, and rise beyond human needs and weaknesses into an angelic or divine station. Noah denies all such claims: a messenger’s claim is only the message, confirmed by a manifest proof from his Lord and accompanied by His mercy. The treasuries of Allah are the hidden resources by which creatures receive provision and remedy their needs.

His wording is significant. “Neither do I know the Unseen” truly negates possession of such knowledge, whereas merely saying that he did not claim it would not do so; knowledge of this kind need not be publicly announced. This differs from his formulations about possessing Allah’s treasuries and claiming to be an angel. The same pattern appears in the command to Muhammad: “I do not say to you that I possess the treasuries of Allah, nor do I know the Unseen, nor do I say to you that I am an angel. I follow only what is revealed to me.” Say, “Are the blind one and the seer equal? So do you not reflect?” (6:50). The first statement denies the superiority people demand, the second limits the messenger to revelation, and the third establishes his real superiority: he sees with God’s sight, while others are like the blind beside one who sees. This is why they must follow him.

The commentary then distinguishes dependence on God from independence. People commonly picture God, angels, prophets, and creatures after the model of an earthly king, his agents, and his subjects: separate beings possessing their powers independently, connected only by laws and relations. This mistakenly makes God a limited being alongside the world and treats creatures’ life, knowledge, and power as their own possessions merely bestowed by Him.

Definitive rational proof, however, establishes the all-pervasive existential poverty of contingent beings. Every contingent being depends upon God in its essence and in the attributes and effects of its essence; independence in any respect would contradict that contingency. God alone is independent, self-sufficient, without deficiency or limit. Therefore, there is no rational objection to a contingent being’s having extensive or even universal knowledge, power, or life, or having limited knowledge and power, provided none of this is independent of God.

The Qurʾan’s assignment of knowledge of the Unseen, giving life and death, and creation exclusively to God negates their independent possession by others. Other verses affirm that God may disclose the Unseen to an approved messenger, that the angel of death takes souls, and that Jesus revived the dead and made a bird by Allah’s leave. Read together, these establish that such attributes may appear in prophets and awliyāʾ only dependently, through God’s making them intermediaries and granting their acts existence. Reports and traditions may therefore affirm knowledge of the Unseen or supernatural power for them, so long as these are not treated as independent of God. To affirm them as independently possessed—even while verbally attributing them to God’s grace—is ghuluww and falls under: “O People of the Book! Do not exceed the bounds in your religion, and do not attribute anything to Allah except the truth” (4:171).

Noah also rejects the elite’s judgment that the people despised by their eyes will receive no good from Allah. Their aristocratic order divides humanity into the powerful, who possess wealth and honor and rule, and the weak, who exist merely to serve them. They regard the weak as deprived of dignity, mercy, and even the possibility of religious happiness. Noah refutes this by declaring that Allah knows best what is in their hearts. Outward weakness is not the measure of divine honor or reward; the decisive matter is the state of the soul and its virtues, whose inner reality only God knows. To deny goodness to someone who may deserve it without proof would be ignorant injustice, making Noah a wrongdoer.

Thus Noah denies both kinds of alleged superiority: he does not claim the extraordinary powers that the elite require in a messenger, and he does not deny divine goodness to the dispossessed believers whom they treat as beneath human dignity. The true measure of religious dignity and divine mercy is the purity and integrity of the heart, not the outward condition that people disdain.
verses.32:
Al-Mizan explains that Noah’s people demand the threatened punishment only after they have failed to refute his arguments or invalidate the truth to which he calls them. Their challenge refers to the “punishment of a painful day” (11:26).

Their speech is reported without fa because it was not an immediate reply to Noah’s preceding words. It came after a long period in which he called them to monotheism, argued with them, and exhausted their excuses. The Qurʾanic presentation gathers exchanges that occurred across centuries: Noah called publicly and privately, night and day (71:5–9), and remained among his people for a thousand-less-fifty years (29:14). This is not anomalous, for the narrator is God, who encompasses time, and the recipient of revelation is granted vision of nations and their ends.

Their meaning is that Noah has prolonged his disputation until they are weary, yet they will not believe. Without admitting their inability to answer him, they abandon argument and demand the harm with which a preacher who has lost hope of being obeyed threatens his audience.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains that Noah’s people demand that he personally bring down the divine punishment he has threatened. He humbly answers that, as a messenger, he has no such power: their affairs belong to God alone, and only Allah can bring the punishment if He wishes. Neither Noah’s warning nor their defiant demand affects God’s sovereignty.

“If He wishes” is a subtle but essential qualification. It affirms God’s perfection and transcendence: nothing governs, compels, or influences Him; He does as He wills. “And you cannot thwart” likewise declares His absolute power while answering their challenge, which implies that they regard themselves as beyond the reach of the punishment.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan explains nuṣḥī as exhortation consisting of words or acts intended for another’s well-being. Ghayy, “perversity,” is foolish conduct arising from a corrupt belief, unlike mere jahl, which may arise without a definite belief. Accordingly, ighwāʾ differs from iḍlāl: iḍlāl diverts someone from the right path while the right objective remains in view, whereas ighwāʾ diverts him and causes the objective itself to be forgotten through ignorant preoccupation.

With respect to God, irāda and mashiyya are generally synonymous. The divine will brings about the empowering causes and prerequisites that make what is willed inevitable; causality itself is an act of that will. Noah’s statement that his exhorting cannot benefit them corresponds to his earlier statement that they cannot thwart God. Their affair belongs to God: if He wills to punish them, none can repel His punishment, and Noah’s advice cannot avail them if God intends, as recompense, to leave them to perversity and thereby fulfill the decree of punishment.

Ighwāʾ is not attributed to God at the outset. It may be attributed to Him as recompense after people disobey, deserve misguidance, and are deprived of the means of guidance, being left to themselves. The verse suggests that before the punishment of annihilation comes, God first consigns such people to misguidance. “He is your Lord, and to Him you shall be brought back” gives the reason for all this: management of their affairs belongs to their Lord, to whom all return. It is neither Noah’s power to bring the punishment nor theirs to prevent it, and his counsel cannot benefit them if God leaves them to the misguidance that precedes their punishment.

The commentary notes, but does not adopt, explanations that take ghayy to mean punishment for disbelief, punishment for misleading others, destruction, or a rhetorical response to a belief that God originally compels servants into error. The verse does not require these interpretations.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan treats this verse as a counter-argument directed at the Meccan accusation that the Prophet fabricated revelation. Ijrām means acquiring an offence or ill-gotten gain, and thus denotes guilt or sin. Noah’s call against idolatry and the arguments reported in this chapter closely resemble the Prophet’s own call and arguments, especially those in Sūrah al-Anʿām. After recounting Noah’s warnings, the discourse naturally turns to the same charge of fabrication raised against the Prophet: he conveys the counsel and proof given by an earlier genuine messenger, whose people rejected him and were destroyed. If he had fabricated it, its sin would be his alone; he bears no responsibility for their conduct.

Al-Mizan rejects the view that the verse remains part of Noah’s direct dialogue with his people, requiring a shift from third-person narration to an address to Noah, because this does not suit the context. “I am absolved of your guilty conduct” affirms the disbelievers’ continuing guilt after decisive proof has confronted them. The Prophet’s guilt is stated only conditionally—if he had fabricated the account—whereas their guilt is certain, because the rational arguments themselves are definitive and their rejection turns them away from faith and good deeds. He is not, in fact, a fabricator.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan explains lā tabtaʾis as a command not to grieve with the resigned sadness denoted by ibtiʾās. God informs Noah that no further disbelievers among his people will believe; therefore he need no longer exhaust himself in calling them, except to complete the argument and leave them no excuse. The command consoles him that he has fulfilled his duty, protects him from grief over the long persecution of himself and the believers, and signals that God’s judgement between them is near.

The exception, “except those who already have faith,” concerns only the fact that the disbelievers will not subsequently believe. It does not prove that the believers’ faith would necessarily remain steadfast, as some commentators maintain.

The commentary deduces that worldly punishment does not descend while belief remains possible; once disbelief is rooted in hearts corrupted by idolatry, punishment becomes due. Noah’s prayer that no faithless inhabitant remain appears to have come after this revelation and before the command to build the Ark. Since reason alone cannot know the future faith of the disbelievers or their progeny, he could pray for their destruction only after revelation disclosed that they would not believe; God then answered by commanding the Ark and decreeing their drowning.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains fulk as “ship,” singular or plural, and holds that the plural aʿyun, though formally a plural of paucity, here intensifies God’s abundant and close oversight of Noah as he builds the Ark.

The revelation connected with building is not merely the communication of a legal ordinance. It is practical, enabling divine guidance for carrying out the act, supported by the Holy Spirit. God’s prohibition against pleading for the wrongdoers prohibits every request to avert their harm or punishment, including intercession (shafāʿa), because the judgement has been issued irrevocably. Their certain drowning explains this prohibition, and possibly the whole command: Noah is to build under God’s complete supervision and instruction while not seeking to divert the inescapable decree.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan describes ridicule (sukhriyya) as contemptuous derision and belittlement, unlike play, which need not concern sentient beings. While Noah built the Ark publicly, successive groups of his people’s elders (malaʾ), people of consequence, came to mock and disgrace him. Yet he remained patient, continued his call, and established the proof against them without wavering.

Noah’s reply, “If you ridicule us, we shall ridicule you,” answers their mockery as a distinct response. His use of “us,” rather than “me,” indicates that his family and followers supported him and worked with him on the Ark; although the verse names Noah as the object of ridicule, their mockery extended to the believing community whose foundation was Noah himself.

Initiating ridicule is foolish and blameworthy, but answering it in kind may be permissible when it has a rational purpose, such as displaying resolve or completing the argument. Noah’s reply is such a reciprocal response.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan takes “Soon you will know” as continuing Noah’s response: if his people mock the believers, they will be truthfully mocked by being told that they will discover which side receives punishment. “Whom a disgraceful punishment will overtake” is the object of “know,” making the threatened knowledge certain.

The disgraceful punishment is the Flood, the worldly extermination that humiliates them; the lasting punishment is the inescapable punishment of Hell in the Hereafter. The repetition of “punishment,” qualified first as disgraceful and then as lasting, supports this distinction. The alternative reading that treats “Soon you will know” as complete and begins a separate statement afterward seems unlikely in context.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains fār al-tannūr as the oven’s overflowing or gushing. Narrations report that the Flood began with water erupting from the oven; the expression may also be a metaphor for the intensification of God’s wrath. In either case, Noah’s situation continued until the divine decree became fixed and irrevocable, whereupon God commanded him to act. Interpretations identifying “the oven” with dawn, elevated places, or the face of the earth are far-fetched.

God commanded Noah to take a male and female pair of every animal kind, his household except those already sentenced to destruction, and the believers apart from his family. The excluded household members include Noah’s disloyal wife and his son. It appears that Noah initially thought only his wife was excluded, until he was told that his son was not among the household promised salvation because of his unrighteous conduct.

“And none believed with him except a few” means that exceedingly few believed in God alongside Noah. The wording “with him,” rather than “in him,” fits the context of those saved through faith and submission to God’s lordship; “except a few,” without specifying a comparison, emphasizes their extreme scarcity.
verses.41: Al-Mizan distinguishes majrā-hā, sailing or course, from mujrā-hā, propulsion and steering; mursā-hā, always with initial u, means stopping or fixing. Noah addresses either his family and fellow believers or everyone aboard. Apparently, his words are an invocation and majrā-hā and mursā-hā are maṣdar mīmī: he links sailing and anchoring to God’s name for blessing and protection. Those causes save only through divine care, whose forgiveness and mercy preserve the Ark, its passengers, and their continued earthly life. The commentary calls Noah first in invoking God’s sacred name, arguing for monotheism, bringing scripture and law, reforming social classes, and removing contradictions. It remains possible that his companions recited the invocation or that the two terms denote time or place. Al-Zamakhsharī permits one statement or two: the invocation may qualify boarding or independently predicate the Ark’s sailing and anchoring. A narration says the invocation moved and stopped the Ark; Mujāhid is reported to read mujrī-hā and mursī-hā as attributes of God.
verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains that the Ark sailed on the surface amid mountain-like waves, not submerged like a whale. Noah’s son was in maʿzil, a place of withdrawal, separated from his father and the community of believers; this distance explains why Noah “called” rather than merely spoke to him.

Noah’s tender “O my son” urges him to board with the believers rather than remain among the faithless and share their punishment. He did not say, “Do not be one of the disbelievers,” because he did not know that his son’s apparent belief was hypocrisy. He therefore called him to board the Ark.
verses.43:
Al-Mizan explains āwī ilā as taking refuge by attaching oneself to something. Noah’s son rejected the invitation to board, trusting that a mountain would keep him above the Flood. Noah replied that on that day none could protect from God’s decree except one to whom He granted mercy: refuge from God lay only in God, not in a mountain or anything else.

A wave then separated them and the son drowned. The commentary holds that, had the exchange not been interrupted, his disbelief would in any event have become manifest and Noah would have disowned him. The verse also suggests that Noah’s people lived in a mountainous region and were accustomed to ascending its mountains.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains that the earth’s “swallowing” is its absorption of water into its depths, while the sky’s “leaving off” is the cessation of rain at its source. The waters thus receded from the earth’s surface, and the Ark settled on Judi, a mountain or solid ground, completing the account of the Flood.

The commands to earth and sky are creative (takwīnī) commands, like “be!”: they take effect immediately, causing the earth to absorb the water that had sprung from it and the sky to stop raining. The earth and sky thus both subdued the Flood by God’s command. “The edict was carried out” means that God’s promised punishment of Noah’s people was realized through their drowning and the cleansing of the earth from them. In divine matters, qaḍāʾ and the lordly ordinance are one in external reality, whether described as issuing, creating, enforcing, or realizing the command.

“Away with the wrongdoing lot!” means their removal from God’s mercy and generosity. Like the preceding imperatives, it can describe creatively their drowning, humiliation in this world, and loss in the Hereafter; viewed legislatively, it is recompense for rejecting faith and good works with arrogance. The passive formulations—“it was said,” “the edict was carried out”—and the omission of agents convey awe: such acts can only belong to the One who has no partner in His command. The unmentioned agents remain evident from the narrative: God speaks and executes the decree, the earth absorbs the waters, and the Ark settles.

The commentary regards the verse as extraordinarily concise and harmonious. It presents only the sky, earth, waters, Ark, accomplished decree, and wrongdoing people, yet makes every agent and event intelligible; for this reason, scholars of Arabic rhetoric have devoted particular attention to its eloquence.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan holds that Noah’s call to his Lord, though narrated after the Flood’s conclusion, likely occurred immediately after the wave separated him from his son, the ordering serving to complete the account of the great event. The word “called” conveys the anguished cry of one in distress.

Noah regarded his son as an outward believer and therefore as part of the family whom God had promised to save. Had he known him to be faithless, he would not have called him to board, especially since Noah had prayed for the faithless to be removed from the earth. The son’s refusal to board was, in Noah’s understanding, a sin (maʿṣiya), not disbelief (kufr) or its equivalent.

Despite his grief, Noah observed prophetic decorum. He did not explicitly request his son’s salvation; rather, he recalled that his son was of his family and that God’s promise was true, implicitly raising the question of how his drowning accorded with that promise. Addressing God as Lord appeals for mercy, while “my son” and “my family” state his case. By concluding, “You are the fairest of all judges,” he leaves judgement to God. Thus he seeks clarification rather than asserting that his son must be saved; God’s later answer, that the son was not of the family promised deliverance, refutes the implication.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains that Noah’s son was not of the “family” promised salvation: although biologically Noah’s son and ordinarily part of his household, he was not among its righteous members. In “along with your family—except those against whom the edict has already been given,” family means Noah’s nearest relations, except the unrighteous—his wife and son. In God’s reply, “He is not of your family,” it means the righteous members of those relations. Noah himself must have meant this narrower family in his plea, since otherwise his disloyal wife would have invalidated his argument. Reports from the Imāms of the Prophet’s Household support this apparent reading.

The view attributed to some commentators that the son was not of Noah’s religion is not fundamentally defective, but does not fit the context as well and ultimately returns to this meaning: God denies his belonging in the same sense in which Noah affirmed it, namely as a righteous close relation. The reports attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Mujāhid that he was not Noah’s real son, and the proposal that he was merely Noah’s stepson, lack textual evidence. The first also imputes dishonour to a prophet, whereas the Qurʾan repels such imputations; the reference to Noah’s wife’s betrayal establishes only her disbelief, hostility, disclosure of secrets, and aid to the disbelievers. The stepson reading also conflicts with the explanation that he was excluded because he was “unrighteous conduct,” and would make Noah’s supposed ignorance or metaphorical argument before the All-Knowing implausible.

“Indeed he is unrighteous conduct” refers to the son, describing him hyperbolically as the personification of unrighteousness; a variant reading, “he has done an unrighteous act,” supports the same conclusion. The interpretation that it instead condemns Noah’s implicit request is rejected because it does not suit either the preceding denial that the son belongs to Noah’s family or the following prohibition against asking without knowledge.

Noah had not actually asked for his son’s deliverance. His words were not a question, but he stood on the verge of asking, when God’s special concern and supernatural guidance stopped him. The prohibition does not prove that its object has been committed; rather, it warns him not to seek what he could not know, since his son was not among the righteous family. This accords with prophetic infallibility: God watches over prophets and guides them away when they approach what could lead to error. Noah’s later wording, “I seek Your protection lest I should ask You,” also concerns a future act, not an act already performed. Likewise, the warning lest he be among the ignorant is preventative; jāhil can describe a temporary condition, not only a settled habit, and a warning against repetition would have been phrased as a prohibition on returning to a prior question.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan explains Noah’s words as gratitude for God’s intervention: God prevented him from asking about something he did not know and thereby from falling into ignorance. His seeking refuge from such a question, though it had not occurred, is like the command that an infallible prophet seek protection from Satan and his promptings.

The apparent plea for forgiveness and mercy is therefore not essentially repentance for a committed sin, but thanksgiving for the knowledge, discipline, and special protection God granted him. His return to God expresses refuge in divine forgiveness and mercy, which cover human faults, preserve one from ruin, and encompass one’s well-being. Here “sin” (dhanb) extends beyond violating a legal command to every harmful effect brought about by a person, and forgiveness likewise extends beyond covering ordinary sins to every divine covering that gives felicity and harmony.

Thus, “If You do not forgive me and have mercy upon me I shall be among the losers” means that without God’s protection from mistakes, Noah would be lost. It praises and thanks God for guarding him from a potential slip and directing him to the right course.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan holds that salām most likely means safety from punishment, since punishment is mentioned at the verse’s end, though it may also mean a greeting. Likewise, the blessings bestowed on Noah and the nations are not merely worldly enjoyments, but divine favors that guide to goodness, happiness, and a praiseworthy end. The passive “It was said,” without naming the speaker, conveys awe before God’s majesty.

In its immediate setting, the address commands Noah and the few survivors on the Ark to disembark safely from the Flood with abundant blessings, in order to inhabit and repopulate the earth. Yet the commentary also reads it as a general decree for all human beings descended from the Ark’s occupants until the Day of Resurrection, parallel to Adam’s descent to earthly life. It grants earthly habitation, settlement, and provision, promises felicity to those who obey God, and warns of punishment for those who disobey.

Accordingly, humanity is divided into two categories. Noah, those with him, and the righteous nations originating from them receive peace and blessings; “from those who are with you” includes the Ark’s occupants themselves as the beginning of these nations and their righteous descendants. The context indicates that all aboard the Ark will be felicitous and saved in the Hereafter, having been tested and confirmed in faith. The other nations receive worldly provision and afterward painful punishment; they are deliberately excluded from the honored position and generous permission given to the righteous.

The view that the blessed nations are only descendants of those aboard, thereby excluding the occupants themselves, is rejected, as is the claim that “nations” means the animals on the Ark.
verses.49:
Al-Mizan explains that this story, or these stories, belongs to the Unseen revealed to the Prophet. It is true though previously unknown to him and his people, whereas the account preserved by the People of the Book has been distorted from the truth.

The command to be patient draws the lesson of Noah’s story: his people were destroyed, while he and the believers survived, inherited the earth, and prevailed through patience. The Prophet is therefore commanded to remain steadfast for the truth, since the final outcome belongs to the Godwary—those who patiently serve God.
verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that Hūd is called ʿĀd’s brother because he belonged to them by common tribal ancestry. The wording means that God sent Hūd to ʿĀd; the omitted verb of sending is suggested by “to ʿĀd,” which also accounts for its placement before Hūd. “He said” begins as a new statement, as though answering the implied question of what Hūd said to his people.

Hūd’s command to worship Allah requires exclusive worship of Him. The declaration that they have no god besides Him exposes their worship of other alleged deities, their association of partners with God, and their fabricated claim that these beings could intercede for them.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan cites al-Ṭabrisī’s explanation that faṭara originally signifies splitting or bringing forth, and al-Rāghib’s account that fiṭra is origination and, in relation to human beings, the divinely placed capacity to know God and apprehend the realities of faith. It concludes that fiṭra appears to mean bringing something forth from utter nonexistence. Its causative form gives it a specificity not conveyed by “creation,” which can mean forming a shape from pre-existing matter by assembling parts.

Hūd denies seeking a reward from his people in order to remove any suspicion that his call serves his own interests, even at their expense. Yet his call is not aimless: his reward is from God, who originated him. He thus appeals to their reason to recognize that his counsel is sincere and intended to lead them to the truth.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan explains that the promise of copious rain is conditional on seeking forgiveness and returning penitently to God. Here samāʾ primarily means the clouds that overshadow the earth, though it may also mean rain itself; midrār is an intensive form denoting plentiful, continuous, beneficial rain that revives land and its crops, grass, gardens, and orchards.

“Add power to your power” has been understood as adding the strength of faith to ʿĀd’s bodily strength, or as an increase in physical strength; the commentary considers a more general interpretation preferable. The prohibition against turning away as guilty people clarifies that their idolatry is a disobedience inviting divine wrath, from which they must seek forgiveness and return to faith in order to receive mercy, rain, and increased strength.

The verse indicates that Hūd’s people were suffering drought and barren land. It also indicates a complete correlation between human deeds and cosmic events: righteous action multiplies blessings and divine grace, whereas evil invites recurring calamity, anger, misery, and destruction.
verses.53: Al-Mizan explains that ʿĀd answered both elements of Hūd’s call. Their claim that he had brought no manifest proof means that they regarded his message as unsupported by argument or miraculous sign and therefore unpersuasive. They then refused both to abandon the gods they had set up besides God and to believe Hūd or follow his counsel.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan explains that ʿĀd claimed that one of their gods had afflicted Hūd with evil, such as madness, because he had insulted them; they therefore dismissed his call. Hūd answered by publicly repudiating their alleged partners and challenging both them and their gods to plot against him together without delay.

His repudiation is a performative declaration, not merely a report, though it does not imply that he had ever been involved in their idolatry. His challenge was meant to demonstrate their impotence. If the idols possessed knowledge and power, they would have harmed him for his public rejection of them; and if Hūd were not a truthful prophet protected by God, his powerful people could have punished or expelled him.

Hūd calls Allah as witness to show that his repudiation is genuine and free of hypocrisy, and calls his people as witnesses so that they may see their gods’ and their own inability to harm him. The commentary therefore affirms that this challenge is both a logical refutation of the idols’ divinity and a miraculous, manifest proof of Hūd’s truthfulness, especially in answer to their demand for proof. By saying “together,” he seeks to confound them along with all their false gods and show decisively that he is rightly guided while they are astray.

verses.56:
Al-Mizan explains that Hūd’s preceding challenge does not rest on mere fearlessness or self-reliance. By declaring his trust in Allah, his Lord and theirs, he shows that he relies on the God who governs both him and them in all affairs. God’s holding every living being by its forelock signifies His supreme authority and absolute control over all creatures that move upon the earth.

That God is “on a straight path” symbolizes the constant cosmic order by which He governs with justice and wisdom, making truth prevail over falsehood when they confront one another. Thus Hūd’s continued safety among his people after repudiating their idols and challenging them constitutes a miraculous and manifest proof that he is God’s messenger: neither they nor their gods can harm him, because God upholds His religion and protects him.

The commentary also notes the difference between “my Lord and your Lord” and “my Lord is on a straight path.” In the former, Hūd emphasizes the universality of God’s sovereignty; in the latter, spoken while seeking protection from his people, he invokes God as his own Lord and clings to the bond of servitude through which he seeks the answer to his supplication.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan explains that Hūd addresses his people’s settled refusal to believe, evident in their claim that their gods had afflicted him. If they turn away, he has already conveyed all with which he was sent; the argument against them is complete and punishment has become due.

God’s making another people succeed them means, by implication, that He will remove and destroy them and replace them on the earth. This warning follows Hūd’s earlier promise that repentance would bring abundant rain and increased strength, and his warning that persisting in guilt would bring severe punishment. Their destruction would not harm Allah or deprive Him of anything, nor could they prevent it; His watchfulness means that nothing escapes His knowledge or power.
verses.58: Al-Mizan takes “when Our edict came” to mean the descent of punishment, or more specifically the issuing of the divine command for decisive judgment between a messenger and his people. The mercy by which Hūd and the faithful were delivered is the special mercy reserved for believers, entailing support for their religion and salvation from divine wrath and exterminating punishment. The harsh punishment from which they were saved refers to the punishment that enveloped Hūd’s disbelieving people, not to punishment in the Hereafter.
verses.59:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses twice summarize ʿĀd’s story. They denied God’s signs—wisdom, admonition, and miracles that distinguished truth from falsehood—and thereby disobeyed His messengers. Disobeying Hūd amounts to disobeying all messengers, since the prophets called to the same religion. Although it is possible that unmentioned messengers came to ʿĀd between Noah and Hūd, the context does not support that conclusion.

They also followed every jabbār ʿanīd: a tyrant who subjugates others to his will and obstinately rejects the truth. Their following of such tyrants explains their turning away from Hūd. Accordingly, their condition is summed up as denial of the signs, disobedience to the messengers, and obedience to tyrants.

Their being pursued by a curse means that God cast them away from His mercy, as shown by the punishment that overtook them; it may also denote the enduring record and effects of their sins, through which they set a precedent of idolatry and unbelief. The curse on the Day of Resurrection is their eternal punishment. The interpretation that the worldly curse merely consists in later people cursing them is disfavoured; the final declaration that ʿĀd defied their Lord and should be cast away indicates a divine curse. The wording also contrasts their “following” tyrants with being “pursued” by a curse, while the final declaration condenses the preceding account of their disbelief and its consequence.

verses.61:
Al-Mizan explains that anshaʾakum means bringing living beings into existence and nurturing them, while ʿimāra is the opposite of ruin: bringing land into a condition in which its benefits can be obtained. Thus, istaʿmara-kum fī-hā denotes making the earth habitable and useful for human life. God created human beings from earthly matter, completed their development gradually, and instilled in them the impulse to work the earth so as to meet their needs and overcome their deficiencies. The wording implies that they need nothing for their existence and survival apart from God.

Ṣāliḥ's statement is therefore an argument for exclusive worship: God alone created them, settled them on earth, and governs their affairs. It answers the implied question why He alone should be worshipped. Idolaters, however, imagined God too exalted to be reached by their worship or supplications. They consequently worshipped noble created intermediaries whom they believed governed worldly affairs, seeking their favour, fearing their wrath, and treating them as independent powers and intercessors with God. Idolatry thus severs the direct relation between God and human beings and substitutes these intermediaries for Him.

Since God created humanity and made the earth their habitation, He is close to them; none of the causes and processes of the world is independent of Him. He alone is to be worshipped, His pleasure sought, and His wrath avoided, because He creates and administers all things. The command to seek forgiveness and repent follows accordingly: they must seek pardon for worshipping others and return to faith and worship of God. “My Lord is indeed nearmost responsive” supplies the reason for repentance. Contrary to the idolaters' claim, God is close, responsive, and the One God; therefore repentance and forgiveness are obligatory.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan explains that Thamūd's saying that Ṣāliḥ had been a source of hope means that they expected wisdom, excellence, and beneficial action from him and his household; qad kunta fī-nā indicates that this expectation was widespread among them. They had hoped he would serve his community and lead it toward progress and success, but his call to monotheism disappointed them because they regarded it as a novel attempt to alter their way of life.

Their question, “Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worship?”, is a rebuke and explains their disillusionment: idol worship was a sacred, identity-defining inherited custom whose preservation, in their view, secured their heritage, unity, and values. The present tense in “what our fathers worship” links their worship to that of their ancestors as a continuing, uninterrupted practice. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the explanation, attributed to scholars including Rāshid Riḍā in al-Manār, that it simply means “what our fathers used to worship.”

Their grave doubt is a second ground for rejecting Ṣāliḥ: besides viewing abandonment of idolatry as a destructive innovation, they claimed that he had offered no conclusive proof to remove their doubts and establish his truthfulness. Murīb, derived from irāba, denotes suspicion or mistrust of a person arising from grounds for suspicion.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan takes bayyina here to mean a miracle and raḥma to mean the station of prophethood. Ṣāliḥ's question is conditional: if a miraculous sign proves his call and God has granted him a message and commanded him to convey it, who could protect him from God if he obeyed his people by abandoning his mission? It answers both their claim that his call was self-invented and their allegation that he had brought no decisive proof.

“For then you will increase me in nothing but loss” most probably means that their urging him to forsake his mission, return to their religion, and conform to their traditions would only cause him loss, since whatever opposes the truth is loss. It has also been read as meaning that their words confirm that they are in loss, or increase his insight into their loss, but the first reading is more probable.
verses.64: Al-Mizan states that calling her “the she-camel of Allah” is an honorific attribution, like “the House of God” and “the Book of God.” She was a miraculous sign supporting Ṣāliḥ's prophethood, brought forth from a mountain rock by God's permission. Ṣāliḥ commanded his people to let her graze freely in God's land and warned them not to strike, wound, or kill her; if they harmed her, an imminent punishment would seize them.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan explains that hamstringing the she-camel means slaughtering her. The dār is the city in which the people lived, called an abode because its inhabitants were gathered there like a family in its dwelling; interpreting it as the abode of this world is unlikely in context.

Ṣāliḥ's command to enjoy themselves there for three days means either that they should continue their worldly indulgence, which is only brief enjoyment, or enjoy the blessings they had amassed, including appearances, furnishings, food, drink, and base desires. “That is a promise not to be belied” clarifies that this three-day respite is an unfailing promise.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan explains “and from the disgrace of that day” as meaning that God saved Ṣāliḥ and the faithful with him from both punishment and the shameful event of that day, which exposes disgrace and brings embarrassment or dishonour. Alternatively, it may mean that He saved them from the people and from that day's disgrace.

“Your Lord is indeed the All-strong, the All-mighty” supplies the rationale for their deliverance and shifts from third-person speech to direct address. Like the corresponding conclusion to Hūd's story, it emphasizes divine Lordship: the condemned people had abandoned the servanthood placed upon them, denied God's lordship, and proved ungrateful for their Lord's blessings.
verses.67: Al-Mizan explains that jāthimīn means that the wrongdoers fell lifeless on their faces in their homes. In ka-an lam yaghnaw fī-hā, yaghnaw means to dwell in a place, and fī-hā refers to those homes. The final declaration summarizes the narrative: “Indeed Thamūd defied their Lord” sums up Thamūd's state and Ṣāliḥ's mission, while “Away with Thamūd!” sums up their divine recompense.

In ka-an lam yaghnaw fī-hā, yaghnaw means to dwell in a place, and fī-hā refers to those homes. verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains bushrā as “good news,” ʿijl as a calf, and ḥanīdh as meat roasted on hot stones. Of the proposed senses of ḥanīdh—especially meat roasted until its juices and fat drip, or roasted meat generally—the description of a fat calf in Then he retired to his family and brought a fat calf (51:26) supports the former.

The emphatic opening Certainly (la-qad) Our messengers came continues the preceding prophetic narratives. Al-Ṭabrisī, in Majmaʿ al-Bayān, says that the lām is emphatic and qad suggests an audience awaiting one story of prophets after another. The messengers were angels sent both to give Abraham good news and to destroy Lot’s people. Since rusul is a plural, they numbered at least three; traditions from the Household of the Prophet report four.

The verse does not expressly identify the good news. Elsewhere good news is given to Abraham, though those accounts do not specify whether it concerns Isaac, Ishmael, or both; this chapter’s context suggests Isaac. The exchanged “Peace” means that the angels greeted Abraham and he returned their greeting. Abraham’s indefinite nominative salāmun may convey peace generally or magnify it; compared with the angels’ accusative salāman, it is considered more eloquent and shows his especially generous greeting of those he took to be guests.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan explains that the guests’ failure to reach for Abraham’s offered food conventionally suggested hostility or evil intent, so he mistrusted them. Awjasa min-hum khīfa denotes an inward apprehension rather than an outward display of fear: ījās is fear experienced within the heart, like a faint inner sound. The angels therefore hastened to reassure him, saying that they had been sent to Lot’s people. Once they spoke, Abraham recognized that they were angels, spiritual beings with no need to eat or drink, on an important mission.

This fear does not conflict with prophetic ʿiṣma. Fear is a natural response to what appears harmful and prompts self-protection; it becomes blameworthy only when it overwhelms thought and planning, producing panic and confusion. That vice is cowardice, whereas the absence of all fear in danger is recklessness. Natural sensation and desire enable creatures to seek benefit and repel harm, but they can fall into excess or deficiency. Courage (shujāʿa) is the moderated virtue in repelling what must be repelled, while chastity (ʿiffa) is the moderated virtue in seeking what should be sought. Recklessness, laziness, cowardice, and unrestrained greed are corresponding vices.

God grants prophets courage, not an absence of natural fear: courage opposes cowardice, which disables deliberation and brings loss. Abraham’s fear was therefore wise apprehension, not cowardice. His record of confronting idolatry, his father and people, Nimrod, and the fire into which he was cast shows that nothing deterred him from striving for God. If he feared for life, honour, or property, it was for God’s sake rather than personal desire.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan first takes ḍaḥikat, usually rendered “she laughed,” to mean that Abraham’s wife menstruated. The subsequent good news is presented as resulting from this sign, which prepared her to accept that she would bear a child. Her being “standing by” emphasizes the unexpectedness: as an old woman, she was merely observing Abraham and the guests when she unexpectedly menstruated.

Most commentators instead understand the word literally. The most plausible literal explanation is that, having feared the guests when they would not eat, she laughed with joy after discovering that they were holy angels and that there was no danger. Other proposed explanations lack evidence, including that she laughed at Lot’s people, at the guests’ refusal to eat, or in astonishment at the announcement of a child; the last requires reversing the apparent sequence so that the good news precedes her laughter.

The good news was that she would bear Isaac and that Isaac would have Jacob. The reading of Yaʿqūb with fatḥa, governed by an implicit preposition, is more likely than the reading with ḍamma, which makes Jacob an explanatory continuation of the good news. Jacob’s name also hints that he would “follow” (yaʿqub) Isaac. The commentary regards this as correcting the Torah’s etymology, which links Jacob’s name to his grasping Esau’s heel, and as a subtle Qurʾanic eloquence.
verses.72:
Al-Mizan explains wayl as an unpleasant loss or calamity that causes regret; invoked as yā waylatī, it figuratively conveys that one is surrounded by such a cause of regret. ʿAjūz means an elderly woman, and baʿal means husband, originally one who manages affairs and is independent of others; it may also denote a master or lord. ʿAjīb describes what astonishes because its cause cannot be understood, and thus commonly applies to rare or unusual events.

Abraham’s wife expresses astonishment and regret at the prospect of an old, barren woman and an old, decrepit man having a child. To people, such an event would seem astonishing and could bring humiliation and scandal through their mockery.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains majīd as the abundantly generous one, majd meaning generosity. The angels’ question, “Are you amazed at Allah’s dispensation?” is a rhetorical rebuke: astonishment arises from ignorance of a matter’s cause, but a matter ascribed to God—who does as He wills and has power over all things—should not be strange.

God had already singled out Abraham’s household with great favours and lofty gifts, so another distinguishing blessing, a child from parents beyond the ordinary age of childbearing, should not seem unlikely. By recalling that Allah’s mercy and blessings continually rest upon the household, the angels remove her confusion. “All-laudable, all-glorious” gives the reason: God is the source of praiseworthy action, generosity, and goodness, and His mercy and blessings overflow upon whichever servants He wills.
verses.74:
Al-Mizan explains rawʿ as fear and horror, and mujādila as persistent argument and questioning intended to make one’s view prevail. After Abraham’s fear subsided and he received the good news of Isaac and then Jacob, he pleaded with the angels concerning Lot’s people in an effort to avert their punishment. The present-tense wording either describes a past state or implies, after “when,” that he began to argue.

The verse apparently indicates that the angels first disclosed their mission to Lot’s people, then gave Abraham the good news, and afterwards informed him of the specific punishment. Abraham then pleaded, but was told that the verdict and punishment were inevitable. Another verse elaborates the exchange: And when Our messengers came to Abraham with the good news, they said, ‘W e are indeed going to destroy the people of this town. Its people are indeed wrongdoers.’ He said, ‘Lot is indeed in it.’ They said, ‘We know better those who are in it. We will surely deliver him and his family, except his wife: she shall be one of those who remain behind’(29:32).
verses.75:
Al-Mizan explains ḥalīm as one who does not hasten to punish or take revenge, awwāh as one who frequently laments the evil he suffers or witnesses, and munīb as one who returns every matter to God.

These qualities explain and praise Abraham’s argument on behalf of Lot’s people. His forbearance made him reluctant to seek punishment for wrongdoers while hoping that they might be guided and reform; he was grieved by their misguidance and approaching destruction and continually turned to God for their salvation. This does not mean that he denied their deserving punishment or defended their wrongdoing.
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains that the angels end Abraham’s plea by telling him to abandon argument and hope for Lot’s people’s salvation, because God’s definitive decree has made their punishment inevitable. “Your Lord’s edict has certainly come” means that the decree has reached an irreversible point and cannot be altered. Though its execution is future, once God has issued the command it cannot depart from what He decreed.

The statement that an irrevocable punishment will overtake them reinforces this: no means can prevent or ward it off, for God’s judgement is final. The emphatic wording of both clauses, and the attribution of the decree to Abraham’s “Lord,” underscore divine authority and persuade Abraham to desist.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains that sīʾa bi-him, in the passive, means that the visitors’ arrival distressed Lot. The idiom ḍāq bi-him dharʿan, literally suggesting a curtailed forearm, means that he could find no means of saving them from calamity. A day described as ʿaṣīb is bound up in intense, inseparable hardship.

The messengers were the angels who had come from Abraham, appearing to Lot as handsome young men. Knowing his people’s inclination to indecency, Lot expected that they would not leave his guests unharmed. His cry, “This is a terrible day,” thus expresses his sense of being surrounded by layered and inescapable distress.
verses.78:
Al-Mizan explains yuhraʿūn as being driven forward forcefully and vigorously. Lot’s people came rushing because their long habituation to sin and indecency had made them audacious, immune to shame, warning, and rebuke. The clause that they had been committing vices aforetime may be read as an aside explaining both their rush toward Lot and their intention to harm his guests. Since mere admonition would not restrain them, Lot offered an alternative to the indecency they sought.

His words, “these are my daughters: they are purer for you,” mean that he offered them in lawful marriage. Aṭhar, though grammatically comparative, here signifies unpolluted purity in a general sense. It cannot mean that he offered them for illicit sexual gratification, for there is no purity in such an act; that reading would contradict both his prophetic station and his command, “Be wary of Allah.” Nor was his purpose merely to avoid personal disgrace, since he could then have confined himself to asking that they not humiliate him concerning his guests.

The commentary rejects the claim that “my daughters” means all the women of his community, on the premise that a prophet is like a father to his people. This is an arbitrary interpretation without linguistic support. It is also at odds with their later response that they had no interest in his daughters: as disbelievers, they would not acknowledge their own women as his daughters, absent unsupported evidence that they spoke mockingly. Likewise, the plural does not prove that Lot meant the community’s women rather than his own daughters. The Qurʾan supplies no evidence that he had only two daughters, and no reliable narration establishes it; the present Torah’s claim cannot govern Qurʾanic interpretation.

The objection that believing daughters could not marry disbelievers is not decisive, since it is unknown whether such a prohibition belonged to Abraham’s law followed by Lot. It is possible that this marriage was then permitted, as it was initially in Islam before later abrogation.

Lot’s appeal to fear Allah, followed by his reference to the humiliation of his guests, was not motivated by tribal partisanship or personal interest. He had long called them away from immorality; by invoking hospitality and the shame of violating a guest, he hoped to awaken their chivalry and honor. His question, “Is there not a right-minded man among you?” is an appeal for someone to defend him and his guests, but they remained unmoved.
verses.79:
Al-Mizan takes this as Lot’s people’s answer to his proposal of lawful marriage instead of indecency: they had no intention of marrying his daughters, and Lot already knew both this and the object of their assault.

Several explanations are reported. Their denial of “interest” may mean that they had no need of the daughters; it may deny a right that would arise through marriage; or it may mean simply that they had no inclination toward women. The commentary holds that the wording, “You certainly know,” is decisive: rather than directly answering Lot, they reminded him of a social norm he knew. They had forbidden approaching women, especially by force, or had ceased approaching them altogether, while treating sexual access to males or boys as permissible.

This accords with the Qurʾanic picture of Lot’s preaching against their desire for men instead of women, their abandonment of the wives created for them, their cutting off the way, and their outrages in gatherings. Social norms establish or deny a recognized right. Thus, the best explanation is that they pointed to their established lack of interest in Lot’s daughters because they were women, while making clear their intention to attack his house; the interpretation based on mere inclination is next most plausible.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan explains āwī as joining or allying oneself with another, and rukn as a support comparable to that which upholds a building. After Lot had urged his people to fear God, appealed to their honor regarding his guests, offered his daughters in marriage, and called for a right-minded defender, no one supported him. Their refusal left him grieving and helpless.

The preferred reading is that “If only I had some power through you” means that he wished a sensible person among them would join his side and help repel their attack. “Or could take refuge in a mighty support” expresses his wish for a strong clan able to protect him. This reading follows the immediate context.

Another interpretation takes bi-kum, “through you,” as “against you”: Lot wished for the strength, capacity, and numbers to resist them and protect his guests. A further view, that he wished to oppose them by his own strength alone, is less consistent with the wording. The proposal that he addressed these words to his guests rather than the townspeople is also rejected, since the sudden change of addressee has no textual indication and would introduce an ambiguity unfitting the Qurʾan’s eloquence.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan explains that the angels disclosed their identity only when the crisis had reached its height: they were messengers of Lot’s Lord, and “They will never get at you” means that the townspeople would not attain what they sought. This corresponds to: Certainly they even solicited of him his guests, whereat We blotted out their eyes (54:37): those gathered at his door to do evil were blinded and left stumbling in confusion.

The angels then ordered Lot to depart during part of the night with his family. Asri means to journey by night, while qaṭaʿin min al-layl specifies a portion of the night. The prohibition on turning round means not to turn away from one’s course or face back. The command therefore urgently directs Lot and his closest people to escape the punishment due upon the town at dawn. Interpretations that “turning back” means worrying over possessions or delaying departure merit little consideration.

“Except your wife; indeed she will be struck by what strikes them” is apparently an exception to the order to set out with his family, not an exception to the command that none turn round. She was to remain behind and suffer the punishment with the people, as also indicated by: ‘… except his wife, We have ordained, will indeed be among those who remain behind’ (15:60).

“Their tryst is the dawn” means that punishment would descend at the beginning of morning, as in: So the Cry seized them at sunrise (15:73). It explains why they must leave at night and underscores the imminence of the danger: “Is not the dawn near?” It is also possible that Lot had urged punishment upon his people, and the angels reassured him that its decreed morning time was near; alternatively, the first statement conveys urgency and the second reassures him in his haste.

The verses do not name the fugitives’ destination. In light of ‘Take your family in a watch of the night; and follow in their rear, and none of you should turn round, and proceed as you are bidden’ (15:65), it appears that the angels did not disclose his final destination, leaving it for later revelation.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan explains that the feminine singular pronouns refer to the land, town, or territory of Lot’s people. Sijjīl most plausibly derives from the Arabicized Persian sang gil, “stones and clay,” though other derivations have been proposed. Manḍūd means arranged or layered, and masmūm means marked. Thus, when God’s edict of punishment—His command to the angels—came, He overturned the land and cities, and rained upon them ordered, marked stones of baked clay, each directed in the knowledge of their Lord to its intended target.

The suggestions that the overturning struck residents while the stones pursued those away from the city, that the city itself became the raining stones, or that the stones fell only afterward to intensify punishment are arbitrary and unsupported by the text. Since Sūrah al-Ḥijr says, So the Cry seized them at sunrise (15:73), their punishment consisted of a blast, overturning, and stones rained upon them. It is possible that this describes a volcanic eruption: a blast and earthquake could overturn the city and shower its people with stones and volcanic debris.

“Never far from the wrongdoers” may threaten the wrongdoers of Mecca, meaning that such stones are not far from them; it may instead refer to the physical nearness of the ruined towns on the route between Mecca and Syria, as indicated by: And indeed, it is upon a path often frequented (15:76), and: And indeed you pass by them at dawn and at night. So do you not apply reason? (37:137-138). The shift from “We” and “Our” to “your Lord” supports an address that warns the Prophet’s people and intensifies the rhetorical force against them. Yet the phrase may also be a general warning that this divine punishment is never far from wrongdoers, with Lot’s people as one instance; even then, the Prophet’s idolatrous people may be its primary addressees.
