verses.84:
Al-Mizan explains that Midian is the city in which Shuʿayb’s people lived, so the mission being assigned to Midian rather than its people is figurative speech; calling him their brother indicates that he belonged to them. Likewise, mikyāl and mīzān denote the instruments of measuring and weighing, while “diminishing” them figuratively means short-changing the goods measured or weighed.

The special mention of this practice shows how prevalent and excessive it was among them and how plainly destructive its effects had become. Shuʿayb’s observation that they were “faring well” primarily refers to God-given prosperity—wealth, abundant provision, low prices, and fertility—so that they had no need to wrongfully take even small amounts from others. More broadly, it may include their endowment with intellect, sound sense, and provision; on this reading, it explains both why they should worship God alone and why they should not corrupt the earth through fraudulent dealing. Their wellbeing should deter them from dishonesty, while fear of the all-embracing day should deter them from disobeying God.

It is also not far-fetched that innī arākum bi-khayr means that Shuʿayb looks upon them with the benevolent concern of a sincere adviser who seeks their happiness; his fear for them would then be an empathetic explanation. The yawm muḥīṭ may be the Day of Judgement or the day of punishment in this world. Its being muḥīṭ means that it is decisive and inescapable: there is no refuge except with God, no helper can repel it, and neither repentance nor intercession will avail on it. Thus Shuʿayb warns that disbelief and wickedness bring an unavoidable punishment which he fears will reach his people.
verses.85:
Al-Mizan explains that īfāʾ is giving another person his full due, whereas bakhs is diminution. The repeated command concerning measure and balance emphasizes a matter on which social life depends. Shuʿayb first forbids short measure and weight, then positively commands giving people their full due and forbids depriving them of what belongs to them. Fair measurement is therefore not merely abstention from an obvious reduction; it restores people’s property to its proper owners.

Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī distinguishes ʿayth, ordinarily used for tangible corruption, from the closely related ʿathī, commonly used for corruption apprehended mentally. “Causing corruption” intensifies the prohibition against acting wickedly on earth. The prohibition can encompass every kind of corruption—killing, wounding, and wrongs concerning wealth, rank, or family—though the context plausibly makes it a particular reinforcement of the ban on cheating in weights and measures.

The commentary grounds this in the reciprocal exchange on which civil society rests. People cooperate and exchange benefits, and financial transactions by measure and weight are among the oldest and clearest forms of that exchange. Buying and selling allow people to estimate their necessities, their expenditure, and the plans by which they order their lives.

Hidden short measure or weight ruins the purchaser’s calculations: it reduces the necessities he obtains while making him spend more of the livelihood he has earned. Deprived of sound planning, he proceeds blindly; this is fasād. Once such dishonesty becomes widespread, mutual trust and security collapse. The harm then reaches both upright and corrupt members of society, including those who deal fairly, and a community of mutual cooperation becomes one of deception and ruined life. This is why God says: W hen you measure, observe fully the measure, weigh with an even balance. That is better and fairer in outcome (17:35).
verses.86:
Al-Mizan takes baqiyyat Allāh, literally a residual or surplus, to mean the legitimate profit remaining to a seller after a transaction, by which he can meet his needs. Exchange originally enabled each party to trade an excess for something needed; when trade became a profession, a merchant could lawfully add profit to capital in return for gathering, transporting, and supplying goods. Buyers accept this because it facilitates exchange, and such profit accords with the community’s natural disposition.

Thus the baqiyya to which God guides people through fiṭra—the lawful profit of trade—is better than wealth acquired by short measure and weight, if they are faithful. A believer benefits from what God has made lawful; what God and human fiṭra do not accept contains neither good nor need. Some hold that “should you be faithful” means faith is needed to recognize the truth of this principle, rather than being an additional condition. Others interpret the remainder as the enduring reward of obedience, which is better for believers.

“I am not a keeper over you” means that Shuʿayb has no control over their lives, actions, obedience, provision, or blessings. He is only a messenger charged with delivering the message; they may choose what benefits them or cast themselves into ruin, while he can neither bring them good nor ward harm from them.
verses.87:
Al-Mizan reads the people’s rhetorical question as a sarcastic rebuke: they claim freedom to choose their religion and manage their property, and deny that Shuʿayb has authority to command them according to his own wishes. His worship may direct him, they say, but neither he nor his worship can direct them. They portray his demand that they abandon idolatry and cease dealing dishonestly as an unwarranted attempt to restrict their religious and economic independence.

Their wording attributes his commands to his worship because it has led him to oppose their idolatry and fraudulent practices. They say that they must “abandon” what their fathers worshipped, rather than simply name idols or gods, to invoke an inherited and established communal tradition. Their reference to doing with “our wealth whatever we wish” rests on the claim that ownership gives every person the right to dispose of property according to his own judgement, without another’s objection.

The mockery lies in connecting his personal worship with a command imposed upon them. But their description of him as “gentle and sensible” is not itself ironic. By emphatically affirming his forbearance and sound judgement, they sharpen their reproach: one of such qualities, they argue, should not undertake what they regard as a foolish infringement of others’ freedom. The commentary therefore rejects the view that they intended by these qualities their opposites, ignorance and waywardness.
verses.88:
Al-Mizan explains Shuʿayb’s “manifest proof” as the sign of prophethood—a miracle establishing the truth of his claim—and his “good provision” as the revealed teachings and laws of prophethood. His reply means that, if he is God’s messenger, supported by such proof and revelation, his call is neither foolish nor an attempt to impose his own authority. God owns all things; human beings are His servants, have no freedom in relation to Him, and must return to Him.

“I do not wish to oppose you in what I forbid you” means that Shuʿayb does not incline toward what he prohibits them from doing, in opposition to them. This answers their charge that he seeks to subjugate them: he seeks reform to the extent of his ability, not a private advantage. His conformity to his own commands demonstrates that the prohibition serves the wellbeing of the society of which he too is a member. The commentary also invokes his statement, I do not ask you any reward for it; my reward lies only with the Lord of all the worlds (26:180), as further evidence that he does not seek to control them for himself.

The commentary distinguishes human freedom among human equals from supposed freedom in every matter. By creation, people possess will and choose between acting and not acting; no peer may dominate another according to personal whim. Yet human beings are social, dependent on cooperation, specialization, rules, and governance. To preserve common interests, each must yield part of his freedom to reciprocal rights, laws, and customs. Regulation of matters bearing on public welfare is therefore not enslavement. Similarly, one who advises and forbids socially harmful conduct does not thereby tyrannize over others: the command arises from common interests, and he is merely its messenger.

More fundamentally, people are not free in relation to the universal causal order that formed and surrounds them. Their choices are realized only insofar as causes permit; their needs, faculties, and obligations direct them to the real benefits necessary for life, such as food, shelter, protection, and defence from harm. Their innate need for social life likewise requires reciprocal rights and shared laws. Whether rules are established by a majority, delegates, a ruler, or God and His messenger, they restrict some freedom in order to preserve what remains. Hence a person is free only in relation to peers and only within the scope of personal inclination, not against the necessities of human wellbeing, social welfare, or the causal order.

These realities accord with divine oneness: God is the absolute Owner, while human beings are servants with relative freedom only in relation to one another. He is the absolute ruler, and His messengers, those vested with authority, and the faithful may command, prohibit, and call to obedience by His right. There is no freedom against the truth which they bring.

Shuʿayb’s statement that his success is only with Allah denies independent power even while affirming his effort to reform. Whatever ability he has and whatever external causes are aligned through it come from God. God originates things, deeds, and their connections; preserves them and their effects; encompasses and governs them; and sustains their realization. One who knows this must rely on God and turn penitently to Him. Thus Shuʿayb joins his declaration of reform with trust in God and return to Him.
verses.89:
Al-Mizan explains shiqāq as opposition and hostility, while jarm, originally cutting fruit from a tree, came figuratively to denote an evil act. Shuʿayb warns his people not to let their hostility to him because of his message bring upon them a calamity like those that struck Noah’s people through drowning, Hūd’s people through the barren wind, or Ṣāliḥ’s people through the Cry and the quake.

“The people of Lot are not distant from you” most naturally means that not much time separated the two peoples: Lot was contemporary with Abraham and Shuʿayb with Moses, leaving less than three centuries between them. The proposed geographical reading—that the ruined towns of Lot’s people lay nearby and visibly before the Midianites—is unsupported by the context and lacks evidence.
verses.90:
Al-Mizan explains the command to seek forgiveness and turn penitently as seeking God’s pardon for sins and returning in faith to God and His Messenger. God shows mercy to those who repent and seek forgiveness, and He loves them.

Shuʿayb first says “your Lord” in order to direct his people to God’s lordship over them, for lordship is the relation relevant to worship, forgiveness, and repentance. It also stresses that God alone, rather than their alleged lords, is their Lord. In giving the reason for his exhortation, he says “My Lord is indeed all-merciful, all-affectionate.” Since the reason is also praise, and God’s lordship over them has already been established, this expression conveys that their Lord and his Lord is merciful and loving. It further presents the assertion as grounded in Shuʿayb’s own knowledge and experience of his Lord.

Al-Wadūd derives from wudd, a love made manifest through affection, continuing communication, and kindness. God’s love for His servants is visibly expressed in the abundance of His blessings; thus He is indeed al-Wadūd toward them.
verses.91:
Al-Mizan notes that fiqh is deeper and stronger than ordinary understanding, that rahṭ means a man’s clan or people—possibly a group of only three to seven or ten, highlighting its smallness—and that rajm means stoning.

Having been defeated in argument, Shuʿayb’s people offer no counterargument and instead seek to silence and belittle him. Their claim that they do not comprehend much of what he says means that his speech has made no impression on them and is, in their view, pointless. Calling him weak means that they do not regard him as influential enough even to merit serious attention or an effort to understand him.

Their threat to stone him, but for his tribe, means that consideration for his relatives alone restrains them. The reference to this relatively small group implies that they could kill him without fearing retaliation, but honour his family connection. Their final assertion that he is not venerable to them reinforces that he himself possesses no power or standing that would deter them. Their words thus express contempt for both Shuʿayb and his message.
verses.92:
Al-Mizan explains that ẓihrī, literally what lies behind one’s back, denotes what is neglected or forgotten. To put something behind one’s back, wa ittakhadhtumū-hu warāʾ ẓihriyyan, is to treat it as insignificant and leave it unmentioned.

Shuʿayb answers their claim that only regard for his tribe prevented them from stoning him. He asks how they can honour his tribe while paying no regard to Allah, on whose behalf he calls them. Their treatment of God as forgotten is especially blameworthy because his Lord encompasses all that they do in existence, knowledge, and power. The verse reproves their foolish notion just as they had disparaged Shuʿayb’s lowly standing.
verses.93:
Al-Mizan reports that, in Majmaʿ al-Bayān, al-Ṭabrisī defines makāna as the state in which one is capable of an act, denoting strong ability to accomplish it.

Shuʿayb’s words are a severe and confident threat despite his people’s disbelief and rebellion. He challenges them to act with all their power while he acts according to his own duty. A humiliating punishment will soon overtake its proper target, and then they will know whether he or they was the liar. They are told to wait and watch, while he watches with them, for God watches them closely and does not neglect them.
verses.94: Al-Mizan states that, when the divine edict came, God saved Shuʿayb and the faithful with him through mercy, while the Cry seized the wrongdoers and left them lifeless in their homes. Ka-an lam yaghnaw fī-hā means that they were as though they had never dwelt there. Midian was cursed and done away with just as Thamud was cursed and done away with.
verses.95: Al-Mizan states that, when the divine edict came, God saved Shuʿayb and the faithful with him through mercy, while the Cry seized the wrongdoers and left them lifeless in their homes. Ka-an lam yaghnaw fī-hā means that they were as though they had never dwelt there. Midian was cursed and done away with just as Thamud was cursed and done away with.
verses.96:
Al-Mizan explains that the bi in bi ayātinā denotes accompaniment: Moses was sent accompanied by God’s signs. Prophets may receive a miracle in answer to a people’s demand, as Ṣāliḥ received the She-camel, or be supported by signs from the outset of their mission, as were Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad. In Muḥammad’s case, the guidance with which he was sent is the Qurʾan, also called the light sent down with him.

The āyāt given to Moses apparently mean the miracles performed through him. Sulṭān mubīn is decisive proof and rational argument that subdues minds; since it embraces miraculous signs as well as rational proof, its mention after signs joins the general to the particular. It is also not far-fetched that Moses’s manifest authority means God’s having given him mastery over the circumstances of his encounter with Pharaoh’s household, until Pharaoh and his troops were drowned and the Children of Israel saved. The assurances to Moses that God was with him and that he would have the upper hand support this reading. They and similar verses clearly show that his mission concerned not only the Children of Israel but others as well.

The message was directed to Pharaoh and his elite—the leaders who inspire awe—rather than explicitly to all the people. This may suggest that the masses merely followed their leaders’ decrees and had no independent judgment. Pharaoh’s “dictates” are apparently not confined to speech or individual acts, but include the course and method he adopted and commanded while claiming to lead to rectitude. The verse rebuts that claim: his dictates neither arose from truth nor led to it, but were error and ignorance. Rashīd is cognate with rashshād, both deriving from rushd, the opposite of ghayy; although some say rashīd means “one who guides,” the explicit repetition of Pharaoh’s name instead of “his” may further imply Pharaoh’s own lack of rectitude.

verses.98:
Al-Mizan explains that Pharaoh will lead his people into Hell on the Day of Resurrection because their worldly obedience to his command made him their leader, one of those who invite to the Fire. Fa awrada-hum al-nār means that he will lead them into the Fire; its use of the past tense affirms the certainty of this future event.

The commentary rejects the claim that the verse instead refers to their entering the Fire immediately after death, on the grounds that Pharaoh’s clan are exposed to fire “morning and evening” before the Day of Judgment, whereas on that Day they “will enter the severest punishment,” namely Hellfire. Thus the latter is not merely a consequence already realized through their following Pharaoh.

Wird originally denotes water sought by thirsty humans or animals, and awrada means to lead someone to such water. The verse therefore uses a subtle metaphor: the end sought through one’s actions, and the happiness sought by it, resembles water sought to quench thirst. True ultimate happiness is God’s pleasure and paradise; but by following Pharaoh and leaving that path, the Egyptians made the Fire their destination and watering place. What should have been a source of sweet water satisfying thirst became the torment of the Fire, an evil place to which to come.
verses.99:
Al-Mizan explains that, because they followed Pharaoh’s command, God’s curse pursued them in this world, distancing them from His mercy and proximity. Its worldly manifestation was their drowning; or it was the decree, recorded among their deeds, that they would be expelled from mercy, a decree whose effects included drowning and punishment in the hereafter.

Rifd means a gift, originally help or support given to meet a recipient’s need. Thus the evil award conferred on the Day of Resurrection is the Fire in which they will prostrate. “On the Day of Resurrection” may qualify either their being pursued or the curse itself, paralleling “in this”; the sense is that they are pursued by a curse in this world and the hereafter, while the wretched gift is either that curse or the condition of being pursued by it.

The passage then states that chapter 11 continues in English volume 21 and closes with praise to God. An appended biographical note says that ʿAllāmah al-Sayyid Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī was born in Tabriz on 29 Dhū al-Ḥijjah 1321/17 March 1904, into the Ṭabāṭabāʾī family, also called al-Qāḍī, which it identifies as descendants of the second Imām, al-Ḥasan b. ʿAlī. His father died in 1330 (1912); after religious study in Tabriz, he went to Najaf around 1341 (1923).

There he undertook advanced study with Shaykh Muḥammad Ḥusayn Nāʾīnī al-Gharawī and Shaykh Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Gharawī al-Iṣfahānī, whom the note presents as leading authorities in Shia jurisprudence, its principles, and other Islamic sciences, founders of influential schools, and teachers of the marājiʿ al-taqlīd—the highest legal authorities whose rulings others follow. It especially emphasizes al-Iṣfahānī’s influence on Ṭabāṭabāʾī, as well as his philosophical, literary, and poetic distinction, and Nāʾīnī’s political and social influence. Ṭabāṭabāʾī also studied mathematics with al-Sayyid Abū al-Qāsim Jaʿfar Khwānsārī and applied some of his theories in a work on higher mathematics; philosophy and metaphysics with al-Sayyid Ḥusayn al-Ḥusaynī Bādkūbahʾī; and ethics and spirituality with his relative al-Sayyid ʿAlī al-Qāḍī.

The biography portrays these influences as producing a scholar of jurisprudence and its fundamentals, an independent philosopher, and a model of ethical and spiritual perfection, though his scholarly reputation was overshadowed by his standing as philosopher and spiritual man. After teaching higher philosophy in Tabriz from 1353/1934, he moved in 1364/1945 to Qum, where he taught ethics, philosophy, and Qurʾanic exegesis to advanced students until his death on 18 Muḥarram 1402/15 November 1981. It names Murtaḍā Muṭahharī among his most famous disciples.

His principal work is identified as al-Mīzān fī tafsīr al-Qurʾān, a twenty-volume Arabic tafsīr said to underlie his academic prestige and to display his method of explaining the Qurʾan through the Qurʾan itself. The note also lists Uṣūl-i falsafah va ravish-i riʾalism, a comparative study of Islamic philosophy and modern anti-Islamic schools, especially Marxism, annotated by Muṭahharī; and Shiʿa dār Islām, later published in English as Shiʾite Islam, written at Professor Kenneth Morgan’s request to introduce Shiism to the West.
verses.100:
Al-Mizan explains that “These” refers to the preceding narratives, while min indicates that they are only a portion of the accounts of the townships, their regions, and inhabitants. “Still stand” and “mown down” extend the image of crops, some remaining upright and others harvested.

If the words concern the towns themselves, some ruins remained, such as those of Lot’s people, whereas the towns of Noah’s people and ʿĀd had been erased altogether. If they concern the inhabitants, some peoples remained while their destruction was incomplete, such as the peoples of Noah and Ṣāliḥ, whereas others, such as Lot’s people, had their end decreed; only Lot’s family was spared, and Lot was not originally one of them.
verses.101:
Al-Mizan explains that God did not wrong these peoples by punishing and destroying them after their idolatry and transgression; they wronged themselves by associating others with God and abandoning obedience. Where an act has an appointed punishment, either the act or its punishment must be unjust; if the punishment is not unjust, the act that incurred it is unjust.

Their gods, invoked for benefit and protection, could not help when God’s decree and punishment came. Tatbīb means devastation or annihilation, its root sense being cutting off. Their idolatry merited punishment, and, when afflicted, their further pleas to idols were another sin that intensified their ruin. Ruin is attributed to the gods only figuratively: in reality it resulted from the worshippers’ own supplication to them.
verses.102: Al-Mizan takes “such” to refer to the previously recounted destructions of wrongdoing towns as instances of divine retribution. The verse generalizes from those instances: just as God painfully and severely punished the peoples of Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lot, Shuʿayb, and Pharaoh, so His seizing of every wrongdoing township is painful and severe. The earlier cases are therefore a lesson for those who reflect.
verses.103:
Al-Mizan explains that the destruction of earlier wrongdoing towns is a sign for those who fear the Hereafter: it indicates that God will seize criminals after death with a painful and severe punishment, and should move people to guard against His wrath.

The Hereafter is a day for which all humanity is gathered. Its being described as a day “for which” people are gathered makes this total gathering an inherent and purposive feature of the day, rather than a merely future occurrence. No one can be absent, because the reckoning concerns faith and unbelief, obedience and disobedience, happiness and misery, and every person’s deeds are connected both to his own inner states and actions and to the actions of others. Earlier leaders of guidance and misguidance bear responsibility in relation to later followers, and later followers in relation to their predecessors. Divine requital follows God’s decisive judgement only when this comprehensive gathering has occurred.

This distinguishes the final accounting from the isthmus, barzakh. Earthly life is the realm of action; barzakh is a preparatory realm in which a person’s record is completed and in which a preliminary paradise or fire may be experienced; and the Hereafter is the realm of final judgement and eternal recompense. The punishment and enjoyment of the grave are therefore not a complete accounting or final reward and punishment.

“A day witnessed” follows naturally from the universal gathering. Since it is unqualified, Al-Mizan understands it to be witnessed not only by human beings but by all capable witnesses, including angels and jinn.
verses.104: Al-Mizan explains that the Day of Judgement has a fixed term ordained by God. It is deferred only until that appointed time; when the term arrives, no one can repeal His judgement or resist His decree, and the day must occur.
verses.105:
Al-Mizan explains that “the day it comes” refers most directly to the determinate term for which Resurrection has been deferred: when that term comes, no soul among those assembled speaks except with God’s permission. It rejects al-Ṭabrisī’s reading that the pronoun simply refers to Resurrection and recompense as unnecessarily strained. It also rejects Rashīd Riḍā’s treatment of one “day” as a general time and the other as the particular Day, because it makes time an adverb for itself and yields no substantive distinction. It remains possible, where a particular time is treated as an event, for the pronoun to refer to the day itself.

The exception applies properly to speech: no utterance occurs unless accompanied by God’s permission. Although all speech and events always depend on His permission, this becomes a distinctive feature of Resurrection because that day unveils realities. God gathers His servants, removes their veils, and discloses that He alone possesses power, dominion, protection, command, and control. The apparently independent causes, authorities, protections, and benefits on which people relied in worldly life lose their supposed independence.

Reckoning then rests on the inward states and attributes of souls. Speech in this world is a social device for disclosing meanings concealed from others; if minds were directly perceptible, speech would not be needed. Resurrection is such a disclosure of hidden realities: secrets, records, deeds, and the marks of guilt are manifest. The lies of polytheists and hypocrites there are not attempts to deceive God despite exposed realities, but manifestations of dispositions formed by habitual worldly falsehood. Likewise, the inability of some to prostrate manifests arrogance entrenched in their souls, rather than an externally imposed prevention that could count in their favour.

The Hereafter is the realm of recompense, not of voluntary action. In worldly life a person can act or refrain; once an act occurs, its consequences and earned recompense follow necessarily. At Resurrection, persons confront their inseparable deeds, records, witnesses, and Lord. If summoned to speak, they do so compulsorily and in conformity with manifested deeds; their mouths may be sealed while their limbs testify. Excuses cannot alter a requital identical with what one has done. Thus speech there is not a voluntary disclosure that may be freely true or false, but an expression governed wholly by God’s permission and will. This compulsion follows from the transformation of the Unseen into the seen.

The commentary rejects interpretations that restrict permitted speech to morally decent speech or to beneficial speech such as intercession. The Day is not a domain in which good acts are permitted and bad acts forbidden, and the wording does not confine speech to speaking for or about another. It distinguishes verses that broadly affirm or deny questioning and speech from verses categorically denying speech. The former are reconciled by verses permitting those whom God allows and who speak rightly; the latter by understanding this verse to deny free, self-chosen speech, not every compelled manifestation. Rashīd Riḍā’s reconciliation fails because he does not distinguish these categories or explain what speaking by permission means. Proposals that speech is allowed at different stages, places, or times, that only argumentless speech is denied, or that the exception is discontinuous, either fail to explain divine permission or conflict with the categorical wording. The last proposal ultimately returns to the same point: worldly voluntary speech is excluded, while speech caused solely by God’s will remains.

“Wretched” and “felicitous” are opposed states. Felicity is attaining the good that completes a being and gives it delight; for humans it includes bodily and spiritual perfection. Wretchedness is deprivation of that good. Although the wording does not by itself explicitly exhaust all possible categories, the context of universal gathering and the final issue in Paradise or Hell means that even those of diminished capacity, such as children, the mentally ill, or people without clear guidance, must ultimately join one of the two groups. The verse does not determine when felicity and wretchedness become fixed, nor make them innate or irrevocably decreed; its setting amid calls to faith, obedience, and avoidance of sin indicates that deeds facilitate the path to either outcome.

Al-Mizan rejects Fakhr al-Rāzī’s claim that God’s present information about people’s future felicity or wretchedness proves predestination. A true present judgement that someone will possess a quality in the future does not mean he possesses it now or eternally, just as knowing that daylight will come does not make the night bright. Al-Rāzī also transmits a report in which the Prophet tells ʿUmar that everyone will be made easy for what he was created for, but Al-Mizan holds that this does not establish al-Rāzī’s conclusion.

Divine decree does not turn voluntary acts into compelled ones. An act becomes necessary only relative to its complete sufficient cause (ʿilla tāmma), which includes will, means, receptive matter, time, place, and the absence of obstacles; relative to each component, including human will, it remains contingent. Hence an act is necessary in relation to its complete cause while remaining voluntary in relation to the person. Divine knowledge that a person will act freely, or suffer through voluntary disbelief, makes the freely chosen act and its consequence inevitable in that conditional causal order; it does not make the act occur regardless of the person’s choice. God’s knowledge and decree therefore do not nullify free will or establish predestination.
verses.106:
Al-Mizan explains that zafīr wa shahīq figuratively depicts the wretched in the Fire drawing breath in and out violently, prolonging cries and groans under its severe heat and their immense calamity, with a sound like a donkey’s braying. Al-Ṭabrisī reports that zafīr is the beginning and shahīq the end of such braying; al-Zamakhsharī identifies them as exhalation and inhalation; and al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī likewise treats them as closely related violent breathing.

Though the preceding verse uses singular, indefinite terms for the wretched and felicitous in order to make the denial of speech comprehensive, the following verses return to the plural. This accords with the preceding emphasis on the multitude gathered on the Day of Judgement: the wretched and felicitous are groups among that gathered humanity.
verses.107:
Al-Mizan understands khālidīn fī-hā, applied in parallel to the people of Hell and Paradise, to establish their permanent residence. Khulūd originally denotes remaining in one state without corruption; it can be used for long duration, but in this context denotes eternity. “As long as the heavens and the earth endure” reinforces that perpetuity, despite verses stating that the familiar worldly heavens and earth have a fixed end.

The resolution is that the Hereafter has its own heavens and earth, transformed from those of this world and belonging to the enduring realities “with Allah.” Heaven, Hell, their inhabitants, and the heavens and earth of the Hereafter are everlasting, whereas the present cosmic order ends. This both explains how an eternal abode can be linked to heavens and earth and preserves the Qur’an’s affirmations of their permanence. Al-Zamakhsharī alludes to the existence of an otherworldly heaven and earth, but his alternative definition of them merely as whatever lies above and below Paradise and Hell is inadequate: it makes their permanence depend on Paradise and Hell rather than explaining it, and does not account for the plural samāwāt. Al-Bayḍāwī’s objection that this compares one obscure reality to another fails, because both realities are known from revelation; one revealed truth may clarify another. Al-Ālūsī’s appeal to the familiar celestial bodies likewise fails, since the particular realities intended by Qur’anic terms are determined by contemplating the Qur’an as a whole and interpreting ambiguous passages through clear ones, not by lexical usage alone.

The commentary rejects several alternatives. Taking the phrase as a simile for the duration of the Hereafter, or as a conventional idiom for an extremely long time, cannot convey the required eternity when God explicitly declares the worldly heavens and earth finite. Saying that God will add an endless period after their term ends is textually unsupported. Referring the Paradise and Hell here to barzakh conflicts with a context concerned with the gathered Day of Resurrection and its final reward and punishment; barzakhic punishment is exposure to the Fire, not final entry into it. Reading Hell and Paradise as present states of Satanic influence and divine guardianship also does not suit this context of warning and glad tidings about Resurrection, though it may be valid at a deeper level of Qur’anic meaning.

The phrase “except what your Lord may wish” is best read with mā as a relative pronoun, in parallel with “indeed your Lord does what He desires,” rather than as an infinitival clause. It may except something from the perpetual duration, or except from the collective inhabitants those whom God wills to remove from Hell and admit to Paradise. The latter coheres with reports that sinful, disobedient believers may leave the Fire through intercession; mā may refer to rational beings, as elsewhere in the Qur’an. The corresponding exception concerning Paradise cannot negate its eternal gift. Rather, it safeguards divine omnipotence: God remains able to remove its inhabitants, but will not do so because He does not break His promise. Likewise, the inmates of the Fire do not leave unless God wills, for His power is unrestricted; reports that some guilty people leave by His will do not contradict this.

Other explanations of the exception are rejected. It cannot mean an additional degree of punishment or bliss, because that relies on denying the phrase’s perpetuity. It cannot refer to a pre-resurrection limbo, to forms of punishment beyond groaning and wailing, or be read as illā meaning “and,” because these readings lack textual or grammatical support and disrupt the parallel structure. The view that the wretched and felicitous are the same sinful monotheists—first in Hell, then transferred to Paradise—is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir b. ʿAbd Allāh, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, and some Successors, but conflicts with the context’s exhaustive division of the gathered people into the people of Hell and the people of Paradise. A more general version can treat the division as comprehensive while applying the exception to sinful monotheists removed from the Fire.

The explanation that the exception merely emphasizes an eternity God will never interrupt differs from the preferred view only by making that emphasis its point rather than safeguarding omnipotence. Salām b. al-Mustanīr al-Baṣrī’s view that it excludes intervals between groups entering their abodes fails because the phrase concerns the end, not the beginning, of their stay. A view reported in Majmaʿ al-bayān from Shaykh Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭūsī and some Shīʿī scholars, which connects the verse to grave punishment interrupted before Resurrection, has the same defect as readings that force illā into the sense of “aside from.” Abū Majāz’s view that the exception excludes those forgiven before entering Hell also disrupts the unity of the paired exceptions; forgiven believers are felicitous through their good deeds or intercession and enter Paradise from the outset. “Indeed your Lord does what He desires” both supports the exception and affirms His unrestricted omnipotence.
verses.108:
Al-Mizan notes that “the felicitous” may be read actively, “those who are felicitous,” or passively, “those made felicitous.” The active reading is linguistically more usual because saʿāda is ordinarily intransitive. Yet the passive reading, contrasted with the active form for the wretched, subtly indicates that happiness and goodness come from God, while evil is self-imposed.

ʿAṭāʾan ghayr majdhūdh means a gift never cut off: Paradise is an unending divine bounty. This confirms that “except what your Lord may wish” preserves God’s absolute omnipotence and sovereignty, not that His power has ceased after admitting people to Paradise. He could remove them, but will not, because His promise that they remain there is not broken.

Al-Mizan therefore excludes interpretations that make the exception refer to people who enter Hell and later reach Paradise: some may leave Hell, but no one who enters the eternal Paradise will leave it as an otherworldly punishment. Al-Ṭabrisī reports the Muslim consensus that everyone deserving divine reward enters Paradise and never leaves it. The underlying rational principle is that God must fulfil His promise, since a promise establishes a right for its recipient and failure to fulfil it would be injustice. A threat, by contrast, establishes God’s right to punish, which He may exercise or waive. Thus obedient servants must receive the Paradise promised to them, while God may punish disobedient servants or forgo punishment. The permanence of those admitted to Paradise is further established by abundant Qur’anic and transmitted evidence.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan presents the verse as the conclusion of the accounts of earlier nations destroyed for associating partners with God and spreading corruption. “These” are the Prophet’s people: their idol-worship is blind imitation of their fathers, without proof, and their “share” is the recompense due for their polytheism and transgressions. “Undiminished” (ghayr manqūṣ) reinforces the promise of full payment, indicating that no intercession or forgiveness will reduce their requital.

The commentary considers it more fitting that their “fathers” are the doomed nations of the past—their spiritual predecessors—rather than merely Arab forefathers. Thus the present idolaters repeat the worship of those earlier peoples and will receive their full recompense as those predecessors did.
verses.110:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse compares the disagreement of the Prophet’s opponents about God’s Book with the Israelites’ disagreement about the Torah after Moses. Though disagreement in worldly affairs is natural, disagreement in religion after knowledge has come arises from selfish desire and envy.

Two divine decrees meet here: God’s decree to recompense people for their deeds requires judgement in their disputes, while His decree to let them live and acquire deeds until the Day of Judgement postpones that judgement. Earlier nations were not destroyed merely for disbelief, disobedience, or religious disagreement; their destruction fell under the further decree that, when a messenger comes to a nation, judgement is made among them with justice. Thus punishment for disagreement about the Book is deferred until the Resurrection.

“Grave doubt” (shakk murīb) intensifies the sense of doubt. The commentary holds that “they” apparently refers to the Israelites and “it” to the Torah. Doubt is understandable, since the existing Torah’s transmission terminates with Ezra, who wrote it after the return from Babylon when the earlier Torah had been burned with the Temple; the Gospel has a comparable problem of transmission. Further doubt arises from elements in the current Torah that human nature cannot accept as belonging to a divine book. The alternative interpretation, referring “they” to Arab idolaters and “it” to the Qur’an, is unlikely, because the chapter has already established the Qur’an’s divine origin and challenged them to produce its like.
verses.111:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse emphatically swears that the Lord will fully recompense every one of the differing people for all their deeds, good and bad, since He knows what they do. The grammatical emphases in wa inna kullan lammā la-yuwaffiyanna-hum underscore the certainty and completeness of this requital.

The commentary also considers meritorious a reading reported by al-Ālūsī from Abū Ḥayyān from Ibn al-Ḥājib: lammā is the jussive “not yet,” with its object omitted, yielding the sense that the Lord will recompense fully everyone who has not yet been recompensed for his works.
verses.112:
Al-Mizan explains istiqāma, “going aright,” from the idea of standing upright: a state of balance, stability, and full command over one’s powers. Just as iqāma means establishing something so that its effects are fully realized, istiqāma means seeking a thing’s uprightness and complete effects. For a person, it is the reform and full realization of the self, so that belief, morals, and action do not depart from monotheism. Setting one’s countenance upon religion is therefore istiqāma in it.

The command means that the Prophet must remain steadfast in the religion, fully observing its due, as he has already been commanded elsewhere in revelation to devote himself uprightly to the religion. Al-Mizan rejects al-Ālūsī’s suggestion that “just as you have been commanded” implies an unknown, non-recited revelation: the Qur’an should not be explained through an undisclosed principle when its own prior commands suffice.

It also rejects defining istiqāma as merely the middle course between excess and negligence. It means complete firmness in divine servanthood and full discharge of one’s responsibilities with all one’s capacities. The prohibition, “do not overstep the bounds,” clarifies this: the danger is transgressing the limit of servanthood through arrogance and idolatry, as earlier nations did, not mere failure to observe moderation. Ṭughyān, literally water overflowing its bounds, figuratively denotes such corrupting moral transgression.

“Whoever has turned with you” means the believers who turned back to God through faith, abandoning idolatry; they too are commanded to be steadfast. The Prophet is singled out first in honour of prophethood, although the qualifying phrase “just as you have been commanded” appears directed specifically to him. God’s seeing all that they do grounds the severe warning: they must adhere unwaveringly to monotheism and will be held to account if they violate the command. The separate address to the Prophet also intensifies the weight of his responsibility, which is why many exegetes connect his saying, “Sūrah Hūd has turned me grey,” with this verse.
verses.113:
Al-Mizan explains that rakn and rukūn mean leaning upon or relying on something out of inclination toward it, not merely leaning in a physical sense. Thus the prohibition concerns trusting or seeking support from wrongdoers in matters of religion and religious life: concealing religious truths to please them, abandoning duties they dislike, allowing them authority over communal affairs, or grounding religious and social life in their power or false practices. Such dependence subjects religion to their influence, pursuing truth through falsehood and ultimately destroying truth while trying to revive it.

The verse completes the preceding command not to be among wrongdoers: believers must not approach them by relying on their falsehood. In light of the stories of destroyed peoples, wrongdoing includes following tyrants and the corrupt practices they establish. The expression alladhīna ẓalamū identifies those marked by the wrongdoing of rejecting the divine call, rather than every person who has ever committed an isolated wrong. Yet Al-Mizan rejects the restriction, associated with al-Manār, to the idolatrous enemies of the first Muslims. The particular historical setting does not limit the general wording; the warning includes anyone characterized by wrongdoing—idolater, monotheist, Muslim, or one of the People of the Book. The distinction between verbal and adjectival forms for “those who did wrong” and “wrongdoers” does not establish the restrictive interpretation claimed by others.

The Fire “touching” one who inclines to them is the consequence of relying on their injustice, whereas committing injustice directly entails the Fire itself. On the Day of Judgement no friend besides God will protect such a person; alternatively, the verse means that divine aid will be absent in the state of such reliance. “Then you will not be helped” culminates in disappointment and abandonment.

The prohibition does not include ordinary worldly dealings—such as trade, transactions, or trusting a wrongdoer in a practical matter—when religion and religious life are not founded on that person’s wrongdoing. The commentary notes that the Prophet employed an idolater in connection with his journey from Mecca and Muslims traded with idolaters and disbelievers. Rukūn is also narrower than wilāya: wilāya is nearness that may expose Muslims to an enemy’s religious, moral, or social influence, while rukūn specifically makes the religion or religious life depend on that enemy’s wrongdoing. Every rukūn entails an aspect of wilāya, but not every wilāya is rukūn.

Al-Mizan does not accept the expansive catalogue attributed by Rashīd Riḍā to the direct meaning of rukūn, though it holds that the practices he mentions are improper. Nor does the fact that the Prophet and earliest Muslims were not expected to commit such sins prevent legislative prohibitions from addressing them; the Qur’an also prohibits them from graver acts. The warning is universal to the Prophet and his whole community, early and late alike. Finally, if wrongful practices are incorporated into religion or Muslim communal or personal life, this is no longer merely inclining toward wrongdoers but becoming one of them.
verses.114:
Al-Mizan explains the two ends of the day as morning and evening, and zulfan as the hours of the night nearest the day. The command is thus to maintain prayer at these times, and it accords with the five daily prayers: fajr, ʿaṣr, maghrib, and ʿishāʾ, though scholars differ over the precise distribution of these prayers within the wording. Because the issue bears on jurisprudence, the decisive clarification is to come from the Prophet and the Imams of his household.

Prayer is commanded because it is a good deed that removes the harmful traces of sins—the imperfections they leave upon souls. The principle that good deeds efface misdeeds is therefore an admonition for those mindful of God.
verses.115:
Al-Mizan links the command to patience with the preceding command to prayer, as in: And take recourse in patience and prayer … (2:45). Prayer is a fundamental pillar of worship, and patience a fundamental moral virtue. Together they are the best means of seeking God’s aid in hardship: patience preserves the soul from distress and despair, while prayer turns it toward God and makes it forget its hardship.

Patience includes steadfastness in worship, refraining from sin, and endurance of adversity; it therefore applies to the preceding commands to go aright, avoid transgression and reliance on wrongdoers, and maintain prayer. Yet because this command is addressed specifically to the Prophet, it especially appears to require endurance of the harm inflicted by his people while he calls them to God and of oppression by wrongdoers. By contrast, the command to maintain prayer concerns collective prayer with the believers. God’s not wasting the reward of the virtuous is the reason given for patience.
verses.116:
Al-Mizan takes the question as a rebuke and expression of regret: among the destroyed generations, why were there not people remaining who forbade corruption on earth, reformed it, and thereby preserved their communities from ruin? The exception identifies the few whom God delivered; they were those who did prevent corruption despite the signs and punishments they witnessed.

The rest were wrongdoers who pursued the affluence granted them and became a guilty lot. The verse consequently divides people into the few saved by divine mercy and the criminal majority.
verses.117: Al-Mizan explains that it is not God’s established way to destroy a town whose inhabitants seek good and reform, for that would be an injustice and God wrongs no one. “Unjustly” is therefore a clarifying qualification, not a restriction: it explains why God does not destroy reforming communities, rather than suggesting that He might destroy them in some other unjust manner.
verses.118:
Al-Mizan distinguishes inevitable human differences from the blameworthy difference intended here. Differences of physical constitution, capacities, environment, livelihood, tastes, customs, and social functions are necessary for human life and are attributed to God; they are not censured unless desire drives them against reason. Religious disagreement, however, is not from God. Human beings are created upon a fiṭra that recognizes God and His oneness, and pure religion accords with that fiṭra. Religious division arises after knowledge through envy, hostility, and wrongdoing.

Accordingly, “Had your Lord wished, He would have made mankind one community” means that He could have eliminated religious disagreement and united them upon one creed. “But they continue to differ” concerns persistent disagreement about the truth, not differences in livelihood, conditions, or merely blind imitation of predecessors. Such disagreement is communal division, doubt, and abandonment of the truth: people fashion false opinions resembling truth in order to obscure it, despite knowing it, out of desire and enmity. Those who adhere to the truth stand outside this condemned division.

“Except those on whom your Lord has mercy” excludes the divinely guided believers, whom God has delivered from disagreement concerning the truth. It does not mean that God has removed ordinary human differences even from them. The mercy is guidance, and “that is why He created them” refers to this mercy, not to discord. Although raḥma is grammatically feminine, the masculine demonstrative can refer to it because verbal nouns may be treated as masculine or feminine.

The commentary rejects the claim attributed to Qatāda that God could have made people one community only by compelling submission and eliminating free will, and the view attributed to Abū Muslim that He could have gathered all humanity in Paradise but instead wished to reward deeds. It also rejects interpretations attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī that the difference is non-religious, and to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and ʿAtāʾ that God created humanity for disagreement. The latter reading becomes conceivable only if “them” refers exclusively to those remaining after the people of mercy are excepted. It further rejects the view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās that humanity was created as two groups, one mercied and undivided and the other unmercied and divided, and Mālik b. Anas’s reported view that they were created so one group would enter Paradise and another Hell.

God’s purpose in creation is mercy—human guidance toward happiness and felicity (saʿāda)—just as worship is an end because of its connection with human flourishing. God does not create people to oppress one another, obscure truth, spread falsehood, and then destroy and eternally punish them. Mercy and guidance come from Him, while malice, discord, and oppression come from people themselves; through rejecting His call, denying His signs, worshipping others, and causing corruption, they render themselves deserving of punishment.

“The word of your Lord has been fulfilled” means that His decree has become actual in reality: “I will surely fill hell with jinn and humans, all together!” It is fulfilled through those who wrong themselves and oppose the truth after knowledge has come to them out of enmity. The “word” is this promise of filling Hell, consistent with God’s declaration concerning Iblis and those who follow him.

verses.120:
Al-Mizan explains that “whatever” is specified as the accounts of the messengers, whether related at length or briefly. Their particular benefit for the Prophet is to strengthen his heart, dispel anxiety, and make him steadfast in calling to truth, uprooting corruption, and enduring his people’s persecution.

The truth that has come “in this” may refer to the present chapter, its revealed verses, or in some way the accounts of the messengers. It includes the realities of the origin and the return to God, and God’s way of sending messengers and spreading the divine call: believers are saved in this life and rewarded with paradise in the hereafter, while wrongdoers receive worldly consequences and everlasting punishment. For the faithful, these truths recall their innate knowledge of the origin, the return, and what concerns them, while the narratives and their lessons admonish them.
verses.121:
Al-Mizan holds that this command addresses the disbelievers and brings the argument against them to a decisive close after the preceding narratives. If, despite their reminders and lessons, they persist in idolatry and corruption and refuse to acknowledge the histories of earlier communities and God’s unchanging decree concerning them, they may continue as they choose. The Prophet and the believers, however, are also acting and waiting, while the disbelievers await the consequences of their deeds; they will soon recognize the truth of God’s news and their own falsehood.

The statement is therefore both a decisive refutation and a warning of the kind contained in the former stories, as in Shuʿayb’s warning that the watchers would learn who would receive a disgracing punishment and who was the liar (11:93).

verses.123:
Al-Mizan explains that, after commanding the Prophet and the disbelievers alike to act and await the outcome, the verse reassures and strengthens the Prophet: the final outcome will turn in his favour against them. The Unseen of the heavens and earth, including the outcomes of both parties’ affairs, belongs solely to God, not to the deities associated with Him or to the means on which the disbelievers depend. All affairs return to God, who discloses from the Unseen their outcomes as He wills and as He has foretold.

The use of the name “Allah” rather than the repeated expression “your Lord” conveys His all-encompassing reality, great and small, and suits a context requiring refuge in One whom none can overcome or surpass. The verse then returns to “your Lord” in saying that He is not oblivious of what they do.

Because every affair returns exclusively to Him and none besides Him possesses or controls anything, He alone must be worshipped and taken as trustee in every matter. Causes operate only by His decree and have no independent power; reliance on them is ignorance. Since the Lord is not unaware of what people do, devotion in worship and reliance upon Him remains imperative.
